title: MMAHP Ch 5-8 — MCIs for OLQ 5-8
sourceFile: MCI for OLQs 5-8 on MMAHP Ch 5-8.pdf

chapters.title: Microbial Metabolism I: Catabolic Reactions for ATP synthesis

questions.stem: Of the 25 essential elements, _________ is a macronutrient and _________ is a micronutrient.

options.text: C/S
N/P
Fe/N
P/I
Se/Cu Carbon fixation: Light-independent reactions of photosynthesis

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Macronutrients are C, N, S, P. Only D pairs a macronutrient (P) with a non-macro element (I). A and B are both macro; C is reversed (Fe is not macro, N is); E is both micro. [§5.1 'Of the 25 essential elements, the cell needs C, N, S, and P in large quantities.' Other elements list includes 'Se, Cl, and I'.] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 5 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Which of the following reactions is showing carbon fixation?

options.text: C + O2 → CO2
CO2 + H2O → H2CO3
CH3COCOOH + CO2 → O2C-CH2COCOOH
CH3COCOOH + CoA + NAD+ → CO2 + CH3-CO-CoA + NADH + H+

questions.answerRationale: Course text: C attaches CO2 to pyruvate (an existing organic molecule) to give oxaloacetate. A and B involve no organic acceptor; D releases CO2. [§5.1.1 'carbon fixation, where a CO2 molecule is attached to an existing organic molecule'; §5.2.1 'Gluconeogenesis may involve carbon fixation'] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 5 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: In the Calvin cycle, which of the following reactions is catalyzed by the enzyme RuBisCo?

options.text: CO2 + Ribulose bisphosphate → 2 Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate.
5 Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate → 3 Ribulose bisphosphate.
6 CO2 + 6 H2O → Glucose + 6O2.
H2CO3 → HCO3- + H+.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: The course text and slide both write the RuBisCo step as CO2 + RuBP -> 2 G3P. (General biology says 3-phosphoglycerate, but the course writes G3P and A matches it.) [§5.1.1 'Coroplasts attach CO2 to the pentose, ribulose bisphosphate (RuBP). This reaction is catalyzed by an enzyme named RuBisCo... breaks down to two molecules of glycaldehyde-PO4 (G3P)'; slide '3 CO2 + 3RuBp -> (Rubisco) -> 6G3P']

questions.stem: Heterotrophs obtain their carbon from any of the following processes EXCEPT ________.

options.text: by predating
by parasitizing
by decomposing
through the Calvin cycle

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Predation, parasitism and decomposition are named; the Calvin cycle is the autotroph route. [§5.1.1 'heterotrophs... obtain carbon from autotrophs and other heterotrophs, as decomposers, parasites, and predators'] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 5 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Challenge question. The land plants process about 123 billion tons of carbon (about 15% of the total atmospheric CO2) each year. How many tons of CO2 do the plants remove from the air, and how much CO2 is in the atmosphere? (Ref: Beer C et al. Science 2010; 329(5993):834-8). Note: The C atom accounts for 27.3% of the mass of CO2 molecules.

options.text: 45,000/ 300,000 Photosynthesis: Light-dependent reactions

questions.answerRationale: Course text: 123 / 0.273 = ~450 billion tons CO2 removed; 450 / 0.15 = ~3,000 billion tons in the atmosphere. Matches B. [Stem arithmetic: C is 27.3% of CO2 mass; 15% of atmospheric CO2.]

questions.stem: Which of these is a photosystem of a chloroplast?

options.text: Chlorophylls, phycobilin, phycoerythrin, phycocyanin, and carotenoids.
Light-harvesting antennae.
The reaction centers.
All these.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: The text builds a photosystem from pigments + antennae + reaction center, so 'All these' fits the intended reading. CONFIRMED BY ELIMINATION on OLQ 5: you picked "The reaction centers" (the runner-up) and Canvas marked it wrong, so a photosystem is more than the reaction center alone. His slide pairs a photosystem with its reaction center, and the pigments and antennae are part of it, so "All these" is the answer left.

questions.stem: All these components of a chloroplast may release electrons. Which of those electrons directly contributes to ATP synthesis?

options.text: Electrons released by water-plastoquinone oxidoreductase.
Electrons released by the photosystem II.
Electrons released by the photosystem I.
All these electrons.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: In the course text only PS II electrons drive the proton-pumping ETC that powers ATP synthase; PS I electrons go to NADPH and WPO's water-derived electrons only refill PS II. The stem's 'directly' points to B, not 'All these'. Re-checked against his Lecture 5 slide 5: Photosystem I is tied to P700 and NADPH synthesis, while Photosystem II is the one tied to the electron transport chain, the proton gradient and ATP synthesis by F0-F1 ATP synthase. The electrons that directly feed ATP synthesis are PS II's. B.

questions.stem: Which of these components of the thylakoid membrane of a chloroplast splits water and releases molecular oxygen?

options.text: PS I.
PS II.
WPO.
F0F1 ATP synthase.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: The text names WPO as the specific enzyme that splits water and releases O2, and the option uses the professor's own acronym, so the most specific correct answer is C. Confirmed correct on your OLQ 5 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Which of these makes the F0F1 ATP synthase of chloroplasts and mitochondria (or E. coli) different?

options.text: The substrate they use in ATP synthesis.
Dependence on proton gradient.
Structure of the enzymes.
None of these.
All these Nitrogen fixation

questions.answerRationale: Course text: The chapter describes the chloroplast enzyme exactly as the respiratory one (same name, same ADP + PO4 substrate, same proton-gradient dependence), so nothing listed distinguishes them: 'None of these'. CONFIRMED BY ELIMINATION on OLQ 5: you picked "Structure of the enzymes" (the pick of one outside reviewer) and Canvas marked it wrong. "All these" would include structure, so it is out too, and his text gives the two enzymes the same substrate and the same proton-gradient dependence. "None of these" is the answer left.

questions.stem: If the cell runs out of nitrogen, which of the following molecules will the cell be able to synthesize?

options.text: Nucleotides.
Amino acids.
Sugars and lipids.
Proteins and nucleic acids

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Nucleotides, amino acids, proteins and nucleic acids all need nitrogen. Sugars and the fatty-acid/glycerol lipids the chapter describes do not. [§5.2.1 amino acids get '-NH2 group... Ammonium ion or glutamine usually donates the -NH2'; nucleotides made 'using ribose, amino acids, CO2, and ATP'; 'Phospholipids and triglycerides are synthesized using fatty acids and glycerol'] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 5 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Only some bacterial species can fix atmospheric nitrogen. Which of the following bacterial genera are endophytic symbiotic diazotrophs?

options.text: Azospirillum.
Azotobacter.
Clostridium.
Rhizobium.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: The text names Rhizobium as the endophytic root-nodule diazotroph; the others are free-living or root-associated. [§5.1.2 'free-living bacteria (such the genera Azotobacter and Clostridium), root-associated bacteria (such as genus Azospirillum), endophytic root nodule bacteria (such as the genus Rhizobium'] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 5 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Technically defined, which of the following is a nitrogen fixation reaction?

options.text: HNO3 + NaOH → NaNO3 + H2O.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Only C starts from N2 gas. A and B start from already-fixed nitrogen (nitric acid, NO2). [§5.1.2 'Haber-Bosch process (i.e., N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3)'; nitrogenases cause N2 'to react with hydrogen to generate... ammonia (NH3). This process, called nitrogen fixation']

questions.stem: Bacteria generate 200 million tons, and humans generate 85 million tons of nitrogen compounds by fixing atmospheric nitrogen every year. Why do humans fix nitrogen?

options.text: Nitrogen compounds created by bacteria are inferior or not available to human use.
Nitrogen compounds produced by bacteria are not enough to meet current demand.
Nitrogen compounds created by bacteria are more expensive than those created by humans.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Stated directly. [§5.1.2 'Bacteria and archaea synthesize about 200-300 million tons... However, it is not sufficient to support the current global population. To meet global demand, an additional 85 million tons'] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 5 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Why is bacterial sulfur acquisition not considered sulfur fixation?

options.text: Because organic sulfur is abundant in soil.
Because sulfur compounds exist as solid chemicals, not as gases.
Because bacteria directly import sulfur compounds in soil capillaries.
Because absorbable sulfur compounds are already available in soil and water.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Fixation in this chapter means pulling an element out of an unusable atmospheric gas (CO2, N2). Sulfur is already present in soil/water as compounds from which absorbable sulfate is released, so D is the best fit. WHY NOT 100%: the intro's definition stresses ATMOSPHERIC gases, which supports B ('solid chemicals, not gases'), though B is weakened because the text also lists H2S, a gas, as a sulfur source. The chapter never states the answer to this question directly. [Ch. 5 intro (PDF p.1) 'carbon and nitrogen fixation (i.e. attaching C and N atoms from atmospheric CO2 and N2 to organic compounds)'; §5.1.3 'Bacteria, fungi, and plants absorb soluble sulfate ions... Sulfur is abundant in the Earth's cr...] SECOND CHECK (his slides, OpenStax, Exam 2 study guide): The slide lists H2S (a gas) as a sulfur source, which further undercuts B ('solid chemicals, not gases'); the text's 'abundant ... not a limiting factor' plus 'absorb soluble sulfate' supports D. Still no source states why sulfur uptake is not called fixation. Exam 2 study guide: 'Acquisition of sulfur, phosphate, and micronutrients' is NOT in the examination (OLQ only). OUTSIDE REVIEW (two other AI reviewers, 2026-10-12): both chose the same answer as this key; they use general biology, not his key, so this does not remove the flag.

questions.stem: Which of the following is/are an organic sulfur source in the soil and water?

options.text: Sulfate esters and sulfonates.
Elemental sulfur.
Iron sulfide.
H2S.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: The text calls sulfate esters and sulfonates organic; H2S, FeS and elemental sulfur are inorganic. [§5.1.3 'Sulfur in the soil exists as organic sulfate esters (R-O-SO3-) and sulfonates (R-SO2-OH)']

questions.stem: Which of these is an inorganic source of phosphorus?

options.text: Phytic acid.
Apatite ores.
Nucleic acids

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Apatite is named as inorganic; phytic acid and nucleic acids are organic. [§5.1.4 'organic compounds such as phytic acid... and as inorganic phosphates, such as apatite'] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 5 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Challenge question: If a cell runs out of phosphorus, which of these will the cell be unable to synthesize?

options.text: Lipids.
Proteins.
Nucleic acids.
Polysaccharides.
None of these molecules.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Nucleic acids have a phosphate in every monomer of their backbone, so they cannot be made without P. Re-checked: OpenStax (paired with OLQ 5) says phosphorus is found in DNA and RNA, and the Ch 5 text gets phosphate from nucleic acids and food. Nucleic acids cannot be made at all without phosphorus, whereas some lipids (triglycerides on his lipid slide) contain none. C.

questions.stem: Which of these organisms is an auxotroph?

options.text: It requires oxygen for cellular respiration.
It requires light energy to synthesize sugar.
It can synthesize all essential precursor molecules.
It cannot synthesize one or more essential precursor molecules.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Definition stated directly; C defines a prototroph. [§5.2 'auxotrophs, because they are incapable of synthesizing some precursor organic compounds']

questions.stem: Which of these is an essential amino acid for the human cell?

options.text: All 20 amino acids the cell needs for protein synthesis.
Hydrophobic amino acids (those insoluble in water).
Histidine, the human cell cannot synthesize it.
Arginine, the human cell can synthesize it.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: An essential amino acid is one the human cell cannot make (the course's auxotroph logic); option C states exactly that about histidine, while D says arginine CAN be made (so not essential) and A contradicts '9 of the 20'. The chapter does not list histidine by name, but the option carries the deciding clause itself. [§5.2 'human cells cannot synthesize 9 of the 20 amino acids'; Fig/ch. logic: essential = must be taken from food] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 5 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: A cell has glucose but no erythrose (a tetrose sugar), which it needs at this moment. Which of these pathways will the cell use to produce it?

options.text: The Krebs cycle.
Gluconeogenesis
Glycolytic pathway.
Pentose-phosphate pathways.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Erythrose is a tetrose; the text names the pentose-phosphate pathway for this interconversion. [§5.2.1 'The cell may interconvert trioses, tetroses, pentoses, hexoses, and heptoses... through the pentose-phosphate pathway']

questions.stem: Which of the following components may produce an amino acid in one step? Note: APS- adenosine phsophosulfate is AMP-SO4).

options.text: Glycerol and CO2.
Pyruvate and APS.
Acetyl-CoA and ATP.
An organic acid and ammonia.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Stated directly; no other option supplies nitrogen. [§5.2.1 'Some amino acids are synthesized by adding an -NH2 group to the organic acids. Ammonium ion or glutamine usually donates the -NH2 group'] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 5 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: If a cell were able to generate UMP, the cell would also be able to generate________.

options.text: UDP, GDP and CDP
UTP, CTP and dTTP
UMP, AMP and CMP Synthesis of template-independent macromolecules

questions.answerRationale: Course text: UTP, CTP and dTTP are all on the UMP branch; GDP and AMP come from IMP. (The caption's 'UDP is first converted to UMP (reaction 8)' appears to be a typo for dUDP -> dUMP; it does not change the answer.) [Fig. 5.7 caption 'UMP is used in the synthesis of UTP and CTP (reactions 1-3). IMP is used in the synthesis of AMP and GMP... dTMP is synthesized from dUMP... dTTP is synthesized from dTMP']

questions.stem: Which of these macromolecules are synthesized through a template-dependent manner?

options.text: The polypeptide chains of the peptidoglycan cell wall.
Phospholipids such as phosphatidyl ethanolamine.
Polysaccharides such as glycogen.
Chromosomal DNA.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Nucleic acids are template-dependent. The cell-wall peptides (A) are a deliberate trap: the text says they are made by transpeptidases, not ribosomes, i.e. template-independent. [§5.2 slide 'Template independent (lipids and... Template dependent (nucleic acids and'; §5.2.1 peptidoglycan oligopeptides 'synthesized by bacterial transpeptidase enzymes (not ribosomes)']

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT necessary for the cell to synthesize glycogen?

options.text: An existing glycogen molecule.
NADH+H+.
Glucose.
UTP.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Glucose, UTP and an existing glycogen molecule all appear in the reactions; NADH does not. [§5.2.1 'Glucose-1-PO4 + UTP -> UDP-Glucose... Glycogen(n) + UDP-Glucose -> Glycogen (n+1) + UDP'] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 5 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Challenge question: Which of the following functions does the penicillin-binding protein (PBP) serve for bacterial cell wall synthesis?

options.text: Synthesis of NAG-NAM disaccharides.
Synthesis of the polypeptide chain attached to NAM.
Transport of NAG-NAM disaccharides to the periplasmic space.
Crosslinking the polypeptide chains of the NAM of two different polysaccharide chains.
Linking the NAG entity of a NAG-NAM disaccharide to a NAM entity of an existing polysaccharide molecule.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Stated directly. E is the glycosyltransferase's job and C is the carrier protein's. Note B is a near-trap: the text says the oligopeptides are made by 'bacterial transpeptidase enzymes' and PBP is a transpeptidase, but the PBP sentence itself names only cross-linking. (Side note: the text says NAG of Lipid II joins a NAM of the old chain, while the Fig. 5.9 caption says NAM-to-NAM; a self-contradiction that does not affect this item.) [§5.2.1 'Finally, a transpeptidase enzyme (also known as the penicillin-binding protein or PBP) cross-links the pentapeptide chains of two NAM entities from two different polysaccharide chains'] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 5 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Which of these antibiotic groups do NOT interfere with bacterial cell wall synthesis?

options.text: Rifamycin.
Carbapenem.
Vancomycin.
Cephalosporin.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Rifamycin is the only one not on the cell-wall list. [§5.2.1 'Several groups of antibiotics (including penicillin, cephalosporin, carbapenem, monobactam, cycloserine, bacitracin, and vancomycin) interfere with bacterial cell wall synthesis'; §5.4 'Rifamycin, an antibiotic, inhibits bacteria...] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 5 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Grossly, which of the phases of the eukaryotic cell cycle is somewhat equivalent to the B period of the bacterial cell cycle?

options.text: S phase.
M phase.
G1 phase.
Interphase.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Both are the non-replicating normal-activity stage. Interphase (D) also includes S phase, which is the C-period equivalent. [§5.3 B period: 'it feeds and conducts normal metabolic activities'; 'Gap 1 (G1) phase: The cell performs all normal physiological activities except genome replication']

questions.stem: If a eukaryotic cell receives a mitogenic signal, the cell enters ______ and replicates DNA.

options.text: S phase
M phase
G1 phase
C period
D period Replication of chromosomal DNA

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Stated directly; C and D periods are bacterial terms. [§5.3 'Synthetic (S) phase: ...replicates the genome. The cell enters the S phase only after receiving a robust growth (mitogenic) signal.'] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 5 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Which of the following pieces of DNA would be replicated in a live E. coli?

options.text: Any dsDNA inserted in the cell.
The chromosome of a mitochondrion.
E. coli chromosome lacking the replicator.
The chromosome of a mitochondrion with the replicator of E. coli.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Only DNA carrying E. coli's own replicator will be replicated by E. coli. [§5.3 'DNA replication must start at the replication origin'; 'The replication origin (replicator) is species-specific... the proteins that recognize and bind the replicator of one species may not recognize the same in another species.']

questions.stem: Which of the following is the last event for DNA replication initiation in E. coli?

options.text: A primase synthesizes an RNA primer.
Helicase loader loads DNA helicases on the ssDNA.
Initiator proteins bind the replicator of the chromosome.
The sliding clamp loader loads the sliding clamp and DNA polymerase III.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Stated directly. [§5.3 '(v) the sliding clamp loader (proteins) loads a sliding clamp and a DNA polymerase III on the primed DNA. This is the end of the initiation event.'] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 5 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: All the following items are events of DNA replication explained. Which of them is a mismatch (incorrect)?

options.text: Primases: Synthesize the RNA primer.
Helicases: Open dsDNA to create ssDNA.
Initiators: Bind the replication origin (replicator).
Topoisomerases: Bind ssDNA created by DNA helicases.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Topoisomerases act on dsDNA knots, not on ssDNA; the other three pairs match Table 5.1. [Table 5.1 'DNA topoisomerases: Cut dsDNA to remove any knots and then ligate and restore dsDNA'] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 5 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Which of the following is a substrate of DNA polymerase III of E. coli (i.e., which of these the DNA polymerase can use for the reaction it catalyses)?

options.text: The 3' OH end of the RNA or a DNA primer.
ATP, CTP, GTP and UTP.
dsDNA template.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Pol III uses the primer's 3' end and dNTPs on an ssDNA template; B lists ribonucleotides (RNA polymerase substrates) and C says dsDNA. [§5.3 'DNA polymerase III adds nucleotides (dNMPs) to the 3' end of the primer'; Table 5.1 'DNA polymerase III: Copy ssDNA']

questions.stem: DNA is being synthesized in an E. coli cell. Which of these is the leading strand?

options.text: The standard is being elongated in one small piece at a time.
The strand is made from many Okazaki fragments.
The strand is being continually elongated.
The bottom template strand.
The top template strand.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Leading strand = continuous elongation; A and B describe the lagging strand; D/E name template strands, not the new strand. [Fig. 5.13 caption 'DNA polymerase III elongates the two original RNA primers continuously'; §5.3 'The new DNA strands synthesized from the initial two primers are the leading strands... subsequent primers in the form of Okazaki fragments...] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 5 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Which of these enzymes replicates most of the chromosomal DNA in E. coli?

options.text: Primases.
DNA ligases.
Topoisomerases.
DNA polymerase I
DNA polymerase III

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Pol III does the bulk copying; Pol I only fills in where primers were. [Table 5.1 'DNA polymerase III: Copy ssDNA while hanging on the sliding clamp'; 'DNA polymerase I: Removes RNA primers and replace it'] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 5 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Which of the following agents inhibits bacterial DNA replication by specifically inhibiting an enzyme?

options.text: Gamma radiation.
UV radiation.
Metronidazole.
Quinolones.
Busulfan.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Quinolones target an enzyme; radiation damages DNA, and metronidazole and busulfan bind/damage DNA itself. [§5.3 'Topoisomerase inhibitors: Some drugs, such as topotecan and quinolones, bind and inactivate the DNA topoisomerases'] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 5 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Which of these DNA sequence elements is the core promoter of a bacterial gene?

options.text: Transcription regulators bind it.
It codes for a protein or a functional RNA.
It makes the RNA polymerase fall off the gene.
The transcription factors and RNA polymerase bind it.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: A describes control elements, B the structural region, C the terminator. [§5.4 'A group of proteins named transcription factors helps RNA polymerase bind the core promoter'; 'transcription regulators bind the gene's control elements']

questions.stem: Which of these bacterial genes can be considered an operon?

options.text: It lacks regulatory elements.
It has core promoter elements at -10 and -35 regions.
It codes for a single protein or a single functional RNA.
It codes for more than one protein and/or functional RNAs.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Stated directly. [§5.4 'some genes (called operons) code for multiple proteins and/or functional RNAs']

questions.stem: Which of these agents can be used to inhibit RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RDRP) of a virus?

options.text: Rifamycin.
Remdesivir.
Tetracycline.
Actinomycin D.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Rifamycin targets bacterial RNA polymerase, tetracycline the 30S ribosome, actinomycin D intercalates DNA. [§5.4 'Various drugs (such as remdesivir and ribavirin) inhibit the RDRP of some viruses']

questions.stem: The nucleotide sequence of the top or coding strand of a bacterial gene is 5’AACCGGTT3’. What is the sequence of the RNA transcribed from the gene?

options.text: 5’AACCGGTT3’
5’AACCGGUU3’
5’TTGGCCAA3’
5’AACCGGTT3’ RNA grooming

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Coding strand with T->U gives 5'AACCGGUU3'. (Options A and D are textually identical; D has a section header fused on.) [Fig. 5.15 caption 'The transcript (pink) has the same nucleotide sequence as the coding strand, except that the Ts are replaced by Us.'] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 5 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Which of the following methods of RNA grooming is defined INCORRECTLY?

options.text: RNA processing: removing useless portions of the pre-RNAs.
RNA splicing: Removing exons and sequentially ligating the introns.
RNA editing: Attaching nucleotides to an RNA after it is transcribed.
RNA modification: Chemically modifying nucleotide bases of an RNA after it is transcribed.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: B swaps introns and exons. A, C and D match the text's definitions of processing, editing ('additional nucleotides are added') and modification. [§5.4 'The process of RNA splicing removes introns and sequentially ligates exons'] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 5 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Which of the following bacterial RNAs are used by the cell without any grooming?

options.text: tRNA transcripts.
mRNA transcripts.
rRNA transcripts.
Any of these RNAs.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Stated directly; bacterial pre-rRNA/pre-tRNA are processed (Fig. 5.18A). [§5.4 'Almost all newly synthesized RNAs (i.e., pre-RNAs) except bacterial mRNAs are groomed'; 'Bacterial mRNAs are used without grooming.'] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 5 attempt 1 (19/20).

sections.heading: Different types of RNAs and the fate of the RNA

questions.stem: Which of the following is a bacterial mRNA?

options.text: It has an RBSs, UTRs, and one or more ORFs
It is found in the 30S or 50S ribosomes.
It is foiled like the letter L
It carries an amino acid

questions.answerRationale: Course text: B describes rRNA, C and D describe tRNA. [§5.5.1 'All mRNAs have untranslated regions (UTRs)... and one or more open reading frames (ORFs)... The UTR at the 5' end contains... ribosome binding site (RBS)'] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 5 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Challenge question: The nucleotide sequence of prokaryotic 16S rRNA is widely used to classify prokaryotes. Where does the 16S rRNA come from, and where can it be found?

options.text: They are transcribed from rRNA genes; they can be found in 50S ribosomes.
They are transcribed from rRNA genes, they can be found in 30S ribosomes.
They naturally occur as soluble RNAs in the cytoplasm of bacterial cells.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: 16S rRNA is transcribed from an rRNA gene and sits in the 30S subunit per the figure. [Fig. 5.21 (rendered PDF p.18): prokaryote 30S = '16S RNA (1,541 nts), 21 proteins'; 50S = 23S + 5S RNA, 34 proteins; §5.4 rRNA is transcribed from rRNA genes] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 5 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Which of the following is a large subunit ribosome of a bacterial cell? See Fig. 5.21 of MMAHP to answer the question.

options.text: It contains 1 molecule of rRNA and 21 ribosomal proteins.
It contains 1 molecule of rRNA and 33 ribosomal proteins.
It contains 2 molecules of rRNA and 34 ribosomal proteins.
It contains 3 molecules of rRNA and 50 ribosomal proteins.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Two rRNAs and 34 proteins is the bacterial 50S. A is bacterial 30S, B eukaryotic 40S, D eukaryotic 60S. [Fig. 5.21 (rendered PDF p.18): bacterial 50S = 23S RNA + 5S RNA, 34 proteins; eukaryotic 60S = 28S + 5.8S + 5S RNA, 50 proteins] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 5 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about a fully folded tRNA is CORRECT?

options.text: The amino acid is attached to its 5’ end.
Its anticodon is made of five nucleotides.
It folds to a cloverleaf (or cross-like) structure.
It contains an acceptor stem, a D loop, a T-psi-C loop, and an anticodon loop.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: A (5' end), B (five nucleotides) and C (cloverleaf; the course says the fully folded tRNA is L-shaped, the cloverleaf is only the 2-D drawing) are all wrong. [§5.5.3 'Different stems and loops of tRNAs are known... D loop, T-psi-C loop, anticodon loop, and the acceptor stem'; 'fold to the shape of the letter L'; amino acid attached 'to the 3'-OH end'; anticodon is 'a triplet']

questions.stem: Challenge question: The anticodon of a tRNA is 5’CCC3’. Which of the amino acids can an AATase use for charging the tRNA? Note: Please see Table 5.2 to answer the question.

options.text: Cys.
Ser.
Gly.
Ile.
Any of these.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Anticodon 5'CCC3' pairs antiparallel with codon 5'GGG3' = Gly; the text says only one amino acid fits, ruling out E. [§5.5.3 'if the anticodon of the tRNA is 5'GGC3', the codon must be 5'GCC3'... alanine (but no other amino acid)'; Table 5.2 'GGG Gly'] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 5 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: The nucleotide sequence of an mRNA is 5’GCCAGGAUGCCCGGGAAAUUUCAGUGACCGAAA3’. What is the amino acid sequence of the protein its ORF encodes? Note: Please identify the ORF of the mRNA by finding the start codon AUG and the stop codon (which can be UAA, UAG, or UGA; then, use Table 5.2 to answer the question.

options.text: met-gly-lys-arg-pro-gly-ser
met-pro-gly-lys-phe-gln
ser-pro-gly-lys-leu-pro-gln
phe-gly-ala-leu-pro-gln-pro

questions.answerRationale: Course text: ORF = AUG CCC GGG AAA UUU CAG UGA -> Met-Pro-Gly-Lys-Phe-Gln. [Table 5.2: AUG Met, CCC Pro, GGG Gly, AAA Lys, UUU Phe, CAG Gln, UGA Stop] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 5 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Which of these amino acids has six codons? Note: Please use Table 5.2 to answer the question.

options.text: Val, Pro and Thr.
Leu, Ser and Arg.
Phe, Tyr and His.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Stated directly. [Table 5.2 caption 'six codons for Leu, Ser, and Arg'] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 5 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: The Start codon is almost always_______ and the initator tRNA always carry the amino caid __________, thus, all newly syntheses proteins have that amino acid at its N terminus.

options.text: 5’UAA3’/Cys
5’UGA3’/His
5’UAA3’/Trp
5’AUG3’/ Met Protein synthesis

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Stated directly; the other options pair stop codons with wrong amino acids. [§5.5.1 'An ORF starts with a start codon (which is usually 5'AUG3')'; §5.5.4 'The initiator tRNA is charged with methionine']

questions.stem: Which of the following is generally the first step of initiation of protein synthesis in a bacterial cell?

options.text: The small subunit ribosome binds an mRNA.
The small subunit ribosome binds a charged initiator tRNA.
The anticodon of the initiator tRNA aligns with the mRNA start codon.
The large subunit ribosome joins the small subunit ribosome and forms A, P, and E sites.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: The figure orders the steps with mRNA binding first. [Fig. 5.23 caption 'A. The 30S ribosome binds to the RBS of an mRNA. B. The initiator tRNA carrying methionine joins the complex... C. A 50S ribosome joins'] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 5 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: The reaction of peptide bond formation between the amino acid of the A site tRNA and the amino acid or peptide chain of the P site tRNA is catalyzed by the enzyme activity (peptidyl transferase activity). Which of these is the peptidyl transferase activity a part of?

options.text: The uncharged tRNA.
The rRNAs in 50S ribosome subunit.
The rRNAs in 30S ribosome subunit.
Ribosomal proteins of the 30S and 50S ribosome subunits.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: The activity is in the 50S subunit and is an rRNA (ribozyme) activity, not protein. [§5.5.4 'the peptidyl transferase enzyme in the 50S ribosome'; §5.5 'most proteins in the cell are synthesized by ribosomal RNA transpeptidases (i.e., ribozymes)']

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT part of the translocation event of translation elongation?

options.text: The A site tRNA moves to the P site.
An amino acid enters the empty A site.
The A site of the 70S ribosome turns empty.
The 70S ribosome moves the mRNA by one codon.
The P-site tRNA becomes uncharged and moves to the E site.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Entry into the A site happens after translocation, and it is a charged tRNA, not a free amino acid, that enters. A, C, D and E are all listed as translocation effects (E's 'becomes uncharged' technically happens at peptide-bond formation just before, but the move to the E site is translocation). [§5.5.4 'the ribosome moves the mRNA by exactly one codon. This process, called translocation, causes the uncharged tRNA to move to the E site... the peptide-carrying tRNA to move to the P site, leaving the A site vacant... Another charge...] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 5 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Which of the following can NOT be reused for protein synthesis immediately after translation termination?

options.text: The newly synthesized polypeptide chain
The 30S ribosomal subunit.
The 50S ribosomal subunit.
The mRNA.
The tRNAs.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Everything except the released polypeptide is named as reusable. [§5.5.4 'The freed mRNA, tRNA, and ribosomal subunits can be reused for the next round of translation.'] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 5 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of protein modification?

options.text: Part of a newly synthesized polypeptide chain is removed.
The newly synthesized polypeptide is acted on by a chaperonin.
The newly synthesized polypeptide is transported to its final destination.
Sugar or phosphate groups are attached to certain amino acids of the newly synthesized polypeptide.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: A is processing, B is folding by chaperonins, C is transport; D matches the definition of modification. [§5.5.4 'processing (i.e., removal of certain regions...) and modification (certain functional groups, such as -PO4, fatty acids, or polysaccharide chains, are attached']

questions.stem: Which of the following antibiotics inhibit RNA transcription by binding the 30S ribosome?

options.text: Rifamycin
Clindamycin.
Streptomycin.
Erythromycin.
Chloramphenicol.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Streptomycin is the only 30S binder listed. Re-checked against his Lecture 5 slide 38: "Binding 30S ribosome particle - tetracycline and streptomycin"; rifamycin is on the transcription slide, and clindamycin, erythromycin and chloramphenicol bind the 50S. Streptomycin is the only 30S binder offered. (The stem says transcription where he means translation.) C. Confirmed correct on your OLQ 5 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Which of the following antibiotics inhibit RNA transcription by binding the 50S ribosome?

options.text: Indinavir.
Quinolone.
Puromycin.
Tetracycline.
Metronidazole.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Puromycin is the only 50S binder among the options (tetracycline binds 30S; indinavir, quinolone and metronidazole do not act on ribosomes). Re-checked against his Lecture 5 slide 38: "Binding 50S ribosome particles - chloramphenicol, erythromycin, clindamycin, linezolid, puromycin"; tetracycline binds the 30S. Puromycin is the only 50S binder offered. (The stem says transcription where he means translation.) C. Confirmed correct on your OLQ 5 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Which of these gives the genotype of a cell?

options.text: All the molecules found in the cell.
The nucleotide sequence of the genome of the cell.
All intact functional RNAs are found inside the cell.
All intact functional proteins are found inside the cell.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Stated directly; functional RNAs/proteins determine phenotype. [§5.5.5 'The nucleotide sequence of the genome determines the cell's (and the species') genotype.']

questions.stem: A bacterial cell has a protein named NtrC. It does not work until a PO4 group is attached to one of its aspartate residues. Is this protein a functional protein?

options.text: Yes, it is already available in the cell.
Yes, it is already synthesized.
No, it is not fully groomed.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Phosphate attachment is modification (grooming); until it happens NtrC is not functional. [§5.5.5 'the majority of the freshly synthesized RNAs and proteins are nonfunctional. They must be groomed'; §5.5.4 modification = '-PO4... attached to certain amino acids'] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 5 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: The cell can regulate gene expression at each of these steps. Which of them most accurately fine-tunes the regulatory measure?

options.text: Post-transcriptional (but pre-translational) level
Post-translational level
Pretranscription level
Transcriptional level
Translational level The lac operon and its regulation

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Post-translational control acts directly on the functional proteins that set the phenotype, at the last layer, and the text singles it out as the fastest response, so it is the best fit for 'most accurately fine-tunes'. Confirmed correct on your OLQ 5 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Which of these can be called an enhancer for the expression of a lac operon?

options.text: lacZ, because it codes for beta-galactosidase, which acts on lactose.
The core promoter, because RNA polymerase and sigma factor bind it.
The CAP site, because CAP (a regulator) binds it and increases the rate of transcription.
Operator, because the lac repressor (a regulator) binds it and prevents RNA polymerase from binding the promoter.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: The CAP site is the enhancer; the operator is the silencer. [§5.5.5 'an enhancer (known as the cap binding site) at the position -61, and a silencer (named operator)... When a transcription regulator binds the enhancer, the rate of transcription increases.']

questions.stem: Which of the proteins is the beta-galactosidase enzyme?

options.text: It can convert lactose to allolactose.
It can import lactose inside the cell.
It can modify/detoxify toxic sugars.
It is coed by the lacY orf the lac operon.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: B is LacY permease, C is lacA transacetylase, D names the wrong ORF. [§5.5.5 'lacZ: It codes for beta-galactosidase, a lactase enzyme that can split lactose to glucose and galactose or isomerize lactose to allolactose.'] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 5 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: When E. coli grows on a medium having glucose but lacking lactose, which of the following must also take place?

options.text: cAMP is present in the cell.
Lac repressor binds to the operator.
The CAP protein is absent in the cell.
The cell has plenty of allolactose in the cytoplasm.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Repressor on operator is stated. cAMP is made only when glucose is low (A wrong), CAP is always present (C wrong), no lactose means no allolactose (D wrong). [§5.5.5 'When E. coli grows in a medium with plenty of glucose but no lactose... the lac repressor, binds the operator (silencer)'; 'When glucose levels are low, the cell synthesizes cyclic AMP'; Fig. 5.27 'levels of CAP proteins and lac ...] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 5 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: When allolactose is present in the cell, which of these events CANNOT take place?

options.text: The CAP binds cAMP and binds the CAP site (the enhancer).
The lac repressor binds the operator (silencer) of the lac operon.
The rate of transcription of the mRNA of the lac operon is at its highest.
The RNA polymerase-sigma factor binds the core promoter of the lac operon more frequently.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Stated directly. A, C and D can occur when allolactose is present (with glucose absent). Note: the text's sentence 'When E. coli grows in a medium that has both glucose and no lactose' is a typo for 'both glucose and lactose' (it goes on to import lactose). [§5.5.5 'once it binds allolactose, lac repressor cannot bind the operator.'] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 5 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Why does the CAP protein not bind the enhancer (i.e., CAP site) of the lac operon when the cell has glucose?

options.text: The cell lacks cAMP in that situation.
The cell lacks allolactose in that situation.
The cell lacks the CAP protein when glucose is present.
The lac repressor binds the CAP site when glucose is present.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: CAP needs cAMP to bind the CAP site, and cAMP is made only when glucose is low. CAP itself is always present (Fig. 5.27), ruling out C. [§5.5.5 'When glucose levels are low, the cell synthesizes cyclic AMP... CAP binds cyclic AMP. It changes the structure of CAP, allowing it to bind the lac operon's enhancer']

sections.heading: Part 1: Microbial Genetics Vertical vs horizontal (i.e., lateral) gene transfer

questions.stem: Gene transfer to offspring of sexual reproduction is ________ gene transfer, but the offspring of such organisms are genetically ____________ identical to each of the parent organisms.

options.text: horizontal/ almost 100%
vertical/ almost 100%
vertical/ about 50%
lateral/ about 50% Genetic and epigenetic variations

questions.answerRationale: Course text (ch 6 intro / Fig. 6.1): sexual-reproduction progeny inherit DNA from two parents, so inheritance is vertical and each parent contributes about half (~50%). Confirmed correct on your OLQ 6 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Which of the following is a mutation?

options.text: A cell gains a chunk of external DNA in one of its chromosomes.
Changes in the nucleotide sequences of a chromosome of a cell.
A diploid cell turns tetraploid.
A cell loses a chromosome.
All these.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.1): mutations are point mutations (changes in nucleotide sequence) AND chromosomal anomalies - gain of non-native DNA (insertion), polyploidy (4n) and loss of a chromosome are all listed.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an epigenetic variation?

options.text: Methylation of the DNA of a gene in a genome.
Acetylation of histones of the chromatin of a genome.
Heritable phenotypic variations due to the methylation of DNA or the acetylation of histones of the chromatin.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (ch 6 intro): epigenetic variations change phenotype through methylation of DNA or histone modification without changing the sequence, and some are heritable. C is the full definition; A and B are only the molecular modifications. WHY NOT 100%: the course says it will not discuss epigenetics, so the exact wording is the professor's; A or B alone could be keyed as 'an epigenetic variation'. OUTSIDE REVIEW (two other AI reviewers, 2026-10-12): both chose the same answer as this key; they use general biology, not his key, so this does not remove the flag.

questions.stem: Mutations may cause each of the following problems EXCEPT__________.

options.text: eliminate the organism from the population
prevent DNA replication or gene transcription
alter the ability to control the expression of certain genes
prevent evolution through natural selection or other processes
prevent translation of an mRNA or change the function of a protein Point mutations

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.2/6.4): mutations help the species evolve ('help the species evolve even in the absence of selective pressure'); they do not prevent evolution. The other options are listed consequences. Confirmed correct on your OLQ 6 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Which of the following is a transversion type of point mutation?

options.text: Parental DNA 5’CCGGAA3’, daughter cell DNA 5’CCGTAA3’.
Parental DNA 5’CCGGAA3’, daughter cell DNA 5’CCGAAA3’.
Parental DNA 5’CCGGAA3’, daughter cell DNA 5’CCGGAAA3’.
Parental DNA 5’CCGGAA3’, daughter cell DNA 5’CCGAA3’.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.1): a transversion swaps a purine for a pyrimidine. GGAA -> GTAA is G (purine) -> T (pyrimidine). B is G -> A, a transition; C and D are insertion/deletion. Confirmed correct on your OLQ 6 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Which of the following point mutations will cause a frame shift?

options.text: Transversion of a nucleotide in the ribosome binding site (RBS) region of a mRNA gene.
Insertion, deletion, or substitution mutations in the 3’ UTR region of a mRNA gene.
Insertion or deletion of one nucleotide inside the ORF of a mRNA gene.
Insertion, deletion, or substitution mutations in the spacer DNA.
Transition of one nucleotide in the ORF of a mRNA gene.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.4): insertion or deletion of one or two nucleotides in the ORF causes a frameshift. Substitutions (E) and changes outside the ORF do not shift the reading frame. Confirmed correct on your OLQ 6 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Which of the following statements (about point mutations in the ORF of an mRNA gene) is a mismatch?

options.text: Silent mutation: The mutation has changed the codon but not the amino acid it codes.
Missense mutations: A mutation changed a codon and the amino acid it codes.
Frameshift mutation: Insertion or deletion of 1 or 2 nucleotides in the ORF.
Read-through mutation: The stop codon changed to a codon.
Nonsense mutations: A codon changed to an anticodon.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.4): a nonsense mutation changes a codon into a STOP codon; 'codon changed to an anticodon' is not a mutation type, so E is the mismatch. Confirmed correct on your OLQ 6 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Which of these defines polymorphism?

options.text: The mutation is rare (<1% of the population has it) and deleterious.
The mutation is common (>1% of the population has it) and neutral or beneficial.
It is a heritable variation stemming from the chemical modifications of DNA and histones.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.1): a mutation found in >1% of the population that is neutral or beneficial is a polymorphism; <1% suggests deleterious.

questions.stem: Single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) is extremely common. If there is one SNP in every 1,000 bp of DNA, how many SNPs are present in the haploid genome of the human subject? Note: Human genome 3.2 billion bp.
questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.1): about one SNP per 1,000 nucleotides; 3.2 billion / 1,000 = 3.2 million, about 3,000,000 (the text also cites ~3,000,000 differences between two people). Confirmed correct on your OLQ 6 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Horses have 64 chromosomes, and donkeys have 62 chromosomes. What will be the karyotype of the mule sired by a horse and a donkey?

options.text: 62 chromosomes.
63 chromosomes.
64 chromosomes.
Depends on which species is the mother or father of the foal.

questions.answerRationale: Arithmetic from the course's haploid/diploid definitions: the horse gamete carries 32 and the donkey gamete 31, so the mule has 63. Not stated in the text; it follows directly from meiosis. Confirmed correct on your OLQ 6 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Which of these chromosomal anomalies is called translocation?

options.text: A segment of native DNA is removed from the chromosome.
A segment of non-native DNA is entered into the chromosome.
A portion of a chromosome moves to another location of the same chromosome.
A segment of a chromosome is replicated repeatedly and retained in the same chromosome.
A segment of DNA of the chromosome is inserted into the same location in reverse orientation.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.1): translocation is 'a portion of a chromosome moves to another location of the chromosome'. Deletion = A, insertion = B, amplification = D, inversion = E.

questions.stem: A DNA polymerase committed a nucleotide substitution mutation in one of the two strands of the dsDNA molecule. If not corrected, which of the following would suffer the consequences?

options.text: The mother cell.
Both daughter cells.
One of the two daughter cells.
The mother cell and both daughter cells.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.2, Fig. 6.5): an uncorrected error is passed on after the next replication; only the cell that receives the mismatched strand carries the mutation, so one of two daughter cells. Confirmed correct on your OLQ 6 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Which of the following would contribute to replication errors the most in an E. coli cell? Note: NTPs- ATP, CTP, etc.; dNTPs- dATP, dCTP, etc.

options.text: The cell contains more NTPs than dNTPs
The DNA polymerase lacks the proofreading function.
There are some DNA-binding agents, such as metronidazole, inside the cell.
The temperature of the surroundings is 25 degrees Celsius, not 37 degrees Celsius.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.2): proofreading by DNA polymerase's 3'->5' exonuclease cuts the error rate to about 1 in 10 million bp; without it errors rise the most. NTP ratio and temperature are not given as major causes; metronidazole only acts on anaerobes. Re-checked against more of the professor's material: the chapter says proofreading cuts the E. coli DNA polymerase III error rate to about 1 in 10 million bp, while mutagens only "increase the error rates" with no size given, and it files chemical mutagens such as DNA-binding agents under DNA damage, not under replication errors. His Exam 2 study guide also lists "compare and contrast DNA replication errors and DNA damage" as separate topics. Losing proofreading (B) is the biggest contributor.

sections.heading: Causes or mutations: Failure of the mismatch repair system

questions.stem: DNA mismatch repair system acts right after DNA replication to correct any non-(G-C) or non-(A-T) base pairs. How does the system correct the mismatch?

options.text: It removes and replaces the incorrect base with the correct base.
It removes the incorrect nucleotide with the correct nucleotide.
It removes a patch of ssDNA around the mismatched base pair, then DNA polymerase fills the gap.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.2, Fig. 6.3B): mismatch repair removes a patch of the new strand around the mismatch and DNA polymerase fills the gap. Confirmed correct on your OLQ 6 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Some DNA-damaging agents and damage mechanisms are listed below. Which of the statements is INCORRECT?

options.text: Methyl mercury: Donates the methyl group to nitrogenous bases (thus damaging DNA).
Gamma radiation: Ionizes water; the ions create reactive chemicals that break DNA.
Water: Removes adenine and guanine bases from nucleotides.
Water: removes the -NH2 group from A, G or C bases.
UV radiation: crosslinks G or A bases.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.2): UV (UVB) cross-links adjacent T/T or T/C bases, not G or A. Methyl mercury alkylation, gamma ionization of water, and water removing -NH2 groups and A/G bases are all stated. Confirmed correct on your OLQ 6 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Gamma radiation damages DNA by all these methods EXCEPT by ________.

options.text: cross-linking bases of DNA
ionizing water to create reactive ions
breaking the sugar-phosphate backbone of DNA

questions.answerRationale: CORRECTED AFTER OLQ 6: you picked "cross-linking bases of DNA" (the guide's old answer) and Canvas marked it wrong, so it is NOT the answer. The chapter text assigns cross-linking to UVB and says gamma/ionizing radiation ionizes water into reactive chemicals that "damage the bases and break the DNA backbone" (Fig 6.4), so the text alone does not explain Canvas's key. That leaves the other two options and nothing settles which one he keyed as the exception. WHY NOT 100%: this is close to a coin flip between "breaking the sugar-phosphate backbone" and "ionizing water to create reactive ions"; his own OLQ 6 Q22 treats "Gamma radiation: Ionizes water; the ions create reactive chemicals that break DNA" as a correct statement, which supports both. If this question comes up again after a later attempt, try the other one.

questions.stem: Which of these bacterial enzymes removes crosslinking bonds between T-T and T-C bases of DNA?

options.text: UV photolyase.
Methyl transferases.
Base excision repair system.
Nucleotide excision repair system.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.2, Fig. 6.6A): E. coli photolyase uses UV energy to remove T=T and T=C cross-links.

questions.stem: Base excision repair and nucleotide excision repair systems do some steps of the repair job and recruit additional enzymes to complete the job. Which of these do they make other enzymes to complete?

options.text: Detection of the damaged base or nucleotide.
Removal of the damaged base or nucleotide.
Removal of the base, or several nucleotides around the damaged nucleotide.
DNA synthesis to fill the gap (created by the removed nucleotides), and ligation of DNA.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.2, Fig. 6.6C/D): the excision systems detect and remove the damaged base/nucleotides; DNA polymerase then fills the gap and DNA ligase seals it (done by other enzymes). Confirmed correct on your OLQ 6 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Which of these types of DNA repair of broken DNA almost always adds mutations to the genome?

options.text: The SSBR system repairs ss DNA nicks.
The NHEJ system repairs dsDNA breaks.
The homologous recombination system repairs dsDNA breaks.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.2): NHEJ 'almost always leads to mutations'; SSBR restores the bond and homologous repair uses a template. Confirmed correct on your OLQ 6 attempt 1 (19/20).

sections.heading: Causes of mutations: Mobile DNA and biological mutagens

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT expected to happen after a bacterial DNA transposon moves?

options.text: Loss of a portion of a chromosome.
Loss of a gene function due to an insertion mutation.
Lateral transfer of the transposon to another bacterial cell.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.3): a transposon moves within the genome; its removal leaves an unrepaired break (loss of chromosome portion) and insertion can disrupt a gene. Moving to another cell is not part of transposition.

questions.stem: Which of these can be considered a biological mutagen?

options.text: Transposons, DNA viruses, and viruses with cancer-causing genes (i.e., oncogenes).
Water, methyl mercury, methyl methane sulfonate, and potassium nitrite.
UV radiation, electron beam, and gamma radiation.
All these.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.3): 'Mobile DNA, DNA viruses, and oncoviruses are potential biological mutagens.' B is chemical, C is physical. Confirmed correct on your OLQ 6 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Which of the following viruses would mutate most readily?

options.text: A virus with a dsDNA genome.
A virus with an ssDNA genome.
A virus with an ssRNA genome.
A virus with a naked helical capsid.
A virus with an enveloped icosahedral capsid.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.6): viral polymerases have limited proofreading; RNA viruses mutate fastest. Confirmed correct on your OLQ 6 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: A porcine influenza virus infected a pig cell. Some progeny viruses had mutated genomes, affecting their hemagglutinin protein. Hemagglutinin is essential for the influenza virus to infect its host cell. Which of these will be the result of this mutation?

options.text: Antigenic drift.
Antigenic shift.
Antigenic drift or demise of the mutant virus.
Antigenic shift or demise of the mutant virus.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.6): point mutations in a virus's genome are antigenic DRIFT (antigenic shift needs two strains with a fragmented genome in one cell). Because hemagglutinin is essential for infection, the mutant may simply not infect and die, so 'drift or demise'. NOTE: the source PDF lettered two options 'C'; the second is really B and has been re-lettered so only the true C (drift or demise) lights up.

questions.stem: A person is infected simultaneously by human and avian influenza viruses. The influenza virus genome is composed of 8 different RNA molecules. Which of the following viruses generated in the cells of the person has undergone an antigenic shift?

options.text: The viruses that have all the human influenza virus genome fragments.
The viruses that have only the avian influenza virus genome fragments.
The viruses that have some human and some avian influenza virus genome fragments.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.6, Fig. 6.15): antigenic shift = progeny with genome fragments from both parental strains.

sections.heading: Fate of foreign DNA entering bacterial cells

questions.stem: A linear piece of dsDNA was introduced into a bacterial cell. The nucleotide sequence of the incoming DNA is NOT at all similar to the nucleotide sequences in the cell's genome. The incoming DNA lacks a replication origin. Which of these outcomes is NOT expected of this event?

options.text: The dsDNA molecule will be destroyed by the cell’s nucleases.
The dsDNA would be randomly inserted into the cell's chromosomes.
One of the two strands of the incoming dsDNA would be recombined into the cell’s chromosome.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.5): foreign DNA with no similarity is destroyed by nucleases or, rarely, inserted non-homologously. Strand replacement by recombination needs similarity, so C is not expected. Confirmed correct on your OLQ 6 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: A linear piece of dsDNA was inserted into a bacterial cell. The nucleotide sequence of the inserted DNA is quite similar to that in the cell's genome. The incoming DNA lacks a replication origin. Which of these outcomes is the most likely outcome of this event?

options.text: The inserted DNA would be entirely destroyed by the cells’ nucleases.
The inserted DNA would replicate and be distributed to the daughter cells.
One of the two strands of the inserted dsDNA would be recombined into the cell’s chromosome.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.5, Fig. 6.10): similar foreign DNA undergoes homologous recombination - one strand replaces part of a chromosome, mismatches are repaired (gene conversion). Re-checked: the chapter says "If the sequence of the foreign DNA is quite similar to the recipient cell's genome, the cell may accept portions of it via homologous recombination ... enzymes of the cell melt the dsDNA and remove one of the two ssDNA strands" and Fig 6.10 says the complex "aligns one of the two strands of the foreign DNA with one of the two strands of the chromosomal DNA". The stem copies that wording ("quite similar"), and the missing replication origin rules out B. C.

questions.stem: Which of these is gene conversion?

options.text: Variation due to mismatch repair of the heteroduplex formed in a homologous recombination event.
When a mutant/nonfunctional gene turns into a functional gene.
When a functional gene turns a mutant/nonfunctional gene.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.5): the heteroduplex from homologous recombination has mismatches repaired by the cell, producing a recombinant gene - 'gene conversion'.

sections.heading: Lateral DNA transfer: Transfection and bacterial transformation

questions.stem: A eukaryotic cell is transformed if it __________, a bacterial cell is transformed if it ________.

options.text: becomes a tumor cell/ receives foreign DNA
receives foreign DNA/ becomes a mutant cell
have mutations of any type/ have mutations of any type

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.5.1): a transformed eukaryotic cell is one turned into a tumor cell; a bacterium that took up foreign DNA is 'transformed'.

questions.stem: Prokaryotic cells that have suffered DNA damage become naturally competent. What can a naturally competent cell do that an ordinary bacterial cell can’t?

options.text: They die from programmed cell death.
They aggressively destroy DNA inserted into them.
They may actively collect and internalize DNA from the environment.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.5.1): damaged bacteria enter competence, which allows them to take up DNA from the environment. Confirmed correct on your OLQ 6 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Which of the following DNA molecules can a competent bacterium pick up and internalize?

options.text: Pure DNA extracted from bacterial cells and dissolved in distilled water.
DNA released by a dead bacterium in the fecal materials of the colon.
DNA was released by a dead archaeon in the mud of a tidal pond.
Viral or plasmid DNA.
Any of these.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.5.1): DNA from dead cells leaks into the environment and competent bacteria take up DNA from the environment; viral or plasmid DNA can also enter. The text sets no restriction on source. Confirmed correct on your OLQ 6 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Someone wants to insert a human gene into E. coli cells. Which of the following processes will be least helpful in achieving her goal?

options.text: Pack human DNA in a lipid vesicle and mix it with the bacterial cell.
Mix human DNA and the cells and momentarily pulse the mixture with a high electric voltage.
Add human DNA to a solution containing anions (such as SO4-2 ions) and mix it with bacterial cells.
Add human DNA to a solution containing some cations (such as Ca+2) and mix it with bacterial cells.
Mix human DNA and the cells and momentarily treat the mixture with high temperature (i.e. 42o C for 30 sec).

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.5.1, Fig. 6.11): DNA and the cell membrane are both negatively charged; CATIONS neutralize the charge, and electric or heat shock lets DNA in. Anions would add to the repulsion. Re-checked against his slides: Ch 6 slide 16, "How foreign DNA can be inserted in cell", lists artificial competence by cations (Na+, Li+, Ca++), heat shock, electric shock (electroporation) and lipid vesicle (lipofection). Anions are not on the list, and the chapter makes cells competent with cations. C is the one that does not help.

questions.stem: Which of the following phages would be most suitable for treating multidrug-resistant bacterial infections?

options.text: A phage that can cause lytic infection but not lysogenic infection.
A phage that can cause lysogenic infection but not lytic infection.
A phage that can cause both lysogenic and lytic infections.
A phage that was isolated from a sewage sample.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.5.2 and the transduction slide 'Lytic infection - as an antibacterial'): a purely lytic phage kills the bacterium; lysogenic phages can integrate and cause lysogenic conversion/transduction.

questions.stem: Which of the following phages is NOT a defective phage? Note: A defective phage particle may infect a bacterium and inject its DNA into the bacterium, but it would not be able to cause a lytic or lysogenic infection.

options.text: The phage particle contains a phage genome that is attached to a fragment of bacterial DNA.
The phage particle contains a fragment of bacterial DNA, not a phage genome.
The phage has its own genome, free of mutations.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.5.2): defective phages carry bacterial DNA instead of, or attached to, the phage genome; only a phage with its own intact genome can complete lytic/lysogenic infection.

questions.stem: Which of the following phages may cause specialized transduction?

options.text: Progeny phages generated from a lytic infection.
Progeny of a (lysogenic) prophage carrying only its own genome.
Progeny of a (isogenic) prophage carrying a portion of host chromosomal DNA.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.5.2): specialized transduction happens when an induced prophage carries a fragment of the host chromosome next to its insertion site. ('isogenic' in the option is a typo for lysogenic.) Confirmed correct on your OLQ 6 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Which of the following plasmids will allow the host bacterium to become resistant to the antibiotic neomycin?

options.text: F fator plasmids.
R factor plasmids.
Diissimilation (D) plasmids.
Bacteriocinogenic plasmids.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (Table 6.1): R factor plasmids carry antibiotic resistance genes. Confirmed correct on your OLQ 6 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Which of these must a plasmid have to survive and perpetuate in a host bacterium?

options.text: A replication origin.
A circular dsDNA genome.
A gene for the pilus protein.
A gene for an antibiotic resistance enzyme.
A gene that codes for a peptide antibiotic (such as colicin).

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.5.3): plasmids contain a replication origin that lets them replicate independently of the host; the other features vary by plasmid type. Confirmed correct on your OLQ 6 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: A Gram-negative bacterium is resistant to ampicillin because of having an F factor plasmid carrying an Amp- resistant gene. Can a Gram-positive bacterium living in the same environment get the plasmid?

options.text: Yes, via conjugation only.
Yes, via transformation only.
Yes, via conjugation or transformation.
No, the bacteria are phylogenetically unrelated.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.5.3): F factor transfer goes to any F- cell ('of the same or even different species'), and the recipient is defined only as lacking an F factor, so a Gram-positive F- cell can receive it by conjugation; plasmid DNA freed from a dead cell can also be taken up by a competent cell (transformation). The earlier key said transformation only. WHY NOT 100%: the course never discusses Gram-positive recipients of an F factor directly. OUTSIDE REVIEW (two other AI reviewers, 2026-10-12): one agreed with C, one chose A on the real-world point that the F plasmid has a narrow host range. Kept C: that argument would make the answer No (D), not A, and the professor's text says F-plasmid recipients pass DNA on "to other F- cells of the same or even different species" while his slide says transformation "can happen to any cell", so A ("conjugation only") contradicts his own text. A stays the runner-up.

questions.stem: Which of these is an F’ bacterium?

options.text: It has an F factor plasmid.
It lacks an F factor plasmid.
It has an F factor plasmid integrated into its chromosome.
It has a free F factor plasmid to which a piece of chromosomal DNA is ligated.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.5.3): F' = a free F factor plasmid with a fragment of chromosomal DNA attached. Confirmed correct on your OLQ 6 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: An F- bacterium may receive part of the chromosomal DNA from which of these bacterial strains?

options.text: hfr.
F+ or F’.
F’ or hfr.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.5.3): Hfr cells pass the F factor plus chromosomal DNA; F' cells carry a chromosomal fragment on the plasmid. F+ passes only the plasmid.

questions.stem: Is bacterial conjugation a form of sexual reproduction?

options.text: Yes, because F+ cells conjugate with F- cells.
Yes, because the process involves gene transfer.
No, because the cells do not fuse to make a zygote.
No, because the DNA transfer is one-way, not mutual.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.5.3): 'Unlike sexual reproduction, conjugation does not involve the fusion of two cells.' Confirmed correct on your OLQ 6 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: A bacterium received DNA from another bacterium via transformation, transduction, or conjugation. What will happen to the DNA in the recipient cell?

options.text: The cell will destroy the DNA using nucleases.
The DNA will perpetuate in the cell as free DNA and pass to its progeny.
The cell will use the DNA for homologous recombination/gene conversion.
The cell will have the DNA randomly inserted into one of its chromosomes.
Any of these outcomes is possible, based on the information on the incoming DNA.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.5, 6.5.3): incoming DNA may be destroyed, recombined (gene conversion), inserted non-homologously, or persist as a plasmid - which one depends on the DNA. Confirmed correct on your OLQ 6 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Which of the following defines or describes genetic engineering?

options.text: Making cheese using cow’s milk and Lactobacillus bulgaricus.
PCR-cloning a growth hormone gene using bovine cDNA.
Producing human growth factor (protein) in bacteria.
Ligating two molecules of DNA in a test tube.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (Section 2 intro / definitions slide): biotechnology = use of living organisms (cheese, A); molecular cloning = copying DNA (PCR, B); recombinant DNA = joining DNA from sources (D); genetic engineering = 'technology of changing the genome of living cells' - bacteria made to produce human growth factor (C). The four options map to those four defined terms. The earlier key chose B (molecular cloning). Re-checked: the chapter defines genetic engineering as "technology of changing the genome of living cells". Only C changes a living cell's genome. D is recombinant DNA, a tool made in a test tube; B is molecular cloning; A is ordinary fermentation. C. Confirmed correct on your OLQ 6 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Cellular DNA is extracted by breaking open the cell wall, destroying the lipid membranes, and denaturing proteins and RNA. Which of the following agents destroys the cell wall?

options.text: Proteinase K or other proteases.
Lysozyme or lyticase.
Phenol or chloroform.
Chelators such as EDTA.
Detergents such as SDS.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.7): lysozyme destroys the bacterial cell wall and lyticase the fungal cell wall; proteases degrade proteins, phenol/chloroform and SDS disrupt membranes/proteins, EDTA chelates metal ions. Confirmed correct on your OLQ 6 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: All these can be used in DNA extraction EXCEPT _______, which is usually used in extracting RNA.

options.text: salt such as potassium chloride
guanidium isothiocyanate
detergents such as SDS
enzymes such as RNases
chelators such as EDTA cDNA synthesis

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.7): RNA extraction uses guanidinium thiocyanate; DNA extraction uses SDS, proteases, RNase and phenol-chloroform (and EDTA/salt in the buffer). Confirmed correct on your OLQ 6 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Which of these is not necessary for cDNA synthesis?

options.text: An RNA template (mRNA, rRNA, tRNA, or synthetic RNA).
NTPs (i.e., ATP, CTP, UTP, and GTP).
Reverse transcriptase (an enzyme).
A primer DNA.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.8): cDNA synthesis needs an RNA template, reverse transcriptase, a DNA primer and dNTPs (dATP, dCTP, dGTP, dTTP) - not NTPs. Confirmed correct on your OLQ 6 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Which of these is a peptide synthesizer?

options.text: It uses amino acids as the raw ingredients.
It uses dNTPs as the raw ingredients.
It uses NTPs as the raw ingredients.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.9.1): peptide synthesizers build polypeptides from amino acids; DNA synthesizers use dNTPs and RNA synthesizers NTPs.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a clone?

options.text: Copies of PCR-amplified DNA produced by two unique primers.
Chicks hatched from unfertilized eggs of a female turkey.
Chicks hatched from fertilized eggs of a female turkey.
Daughter cells and granddaughter cells of a bacterium.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.9 and the cloning slide): PCR copies, binary-fission descendants and parthenogenesis (unfertilized egg) are clones; offspring of fertilized eggs combine two parents' DNA. Confirmed correct on your OLQ 6 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Which of the following steps of a PCR is CORRECTLY described?

options.text: 55 degrees C: The DNA polymerase extends the primers.
72 degrees C: Allows the primers to anneal to ssDNA.
95 degrees C: Denatures dsDNA to ssDNA.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.9.2): 95 C melts dsDNA, about 55 C lets primers anneal, 72 C is the polymerase's optimum for extension. Confirmed correct on your OLQ 6 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: How is RT-PCR different from conventional PCR?

options.text: RT-PCR uses reverse transcriptase to copy DNA; PCR uses DNA polymerase to do the same.
RT-PCR uses cDNA as the template; PCR uses DNA as the template.
RT-PCR uses NTPs to copy DNA; PCR uses dNTPs to do the same.
RT-PCR does not use primers; PCR does.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.9.2): 'PCR using cDNA template is known as RT-PCR'; reverse transcriptase makes the cDNA from RNA beforehand. Confirmed correct on your OLQ 6 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Which of these is necessary for detecting HPV, a DNA virus (extracted from human skin cells) by PCR?

options.text: The virus DNA must be separated from contaminating human DNA and RNA.
The primers should anneal to the viral DNA, not to any other DNA.
The virus must have a linear DNA genome.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.9.2): PCR detects a virus because primers anneal only to their complementary sequence; no purification of the viral DNA is needed. Confirmed correct on your OLQ 6 attempt 1 (19/20).

sections.heading: Vectored cloning: Cloning vectors, DNA ligation, and transfection

questions.stem: Which of the following features must a cloning vector have for it to be able to replicate inside the transfected cell?

options.text: It should contain a multicloning site (MCS) with suitable restriction endonuclease digestion sites.
It should contain marker or reporter genes, such as the ampicillin resistance gene.
It should be a circular dsDNA molecule.
It should contain a replication origin.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.9.3): the plasmid or viral genome 'contains a replication origin', which is why the recombinant vector replicates in the host. Confirmed correct on your OLQ 6 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: In which aspect is vectored cloning superior to PCR cloning?

options.text: Time it takes to finish cloning.
The size of DNA that can be cloned.
Amounts of cloned DNA that can be generated.
Ease of isolating the DNA fragments to be cloned.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.9.3): PCR clones only <20,000 bp; vector cloning can clone fragments of 500,000 bp. Confirmed correct on your OLQ 6 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: The steps of vectored cloning are listed below. Which of these is the third step (from start to finish) of the process?

options.text: Transfect competent E. coli cells using the ligated DNA.
Mix the prepared vector and the insert DNA and add DNA ligase.
Prepare the cloning vector by digesting with the appropriate restriction endonuclease.
Isolate the insert DNA to be cloned; cut it with the appropriate restriction endonuclease.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (vectored-cloning slide / Fig. 6.22): purify and cut the insert (1), cut the vector (2), mix and add DNA ligase (3), transfect E. coli (4), screen.

questions.stem: Which of the following methods of transfection is most suitable for plant cells (in tissue culture)?

options.text: Brief electric shock (also called electroporation).
Brief heat shock (i.e., heat-shock-poration).
Lipid micelles (also called lipofection).
Microinjection.
Gene gun.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.9.3): a gene gun shoots DNA on gold/copper particles into plant cells. Confirmed correct on your OLQ 6 attempt 1 (19/20).

sections.heading: Use of Cloned DNA: Modern DNA sequencing

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT necessary for sequencing DNA if DNA polymerase is used for the purpose?

options.text: Sensors to detect which nucleotide was used for DNA synthesis.
Computer software to record and report the nucleotide sequence.
The four nucleotides; each labeled with a different fluorescent dye.
Template DNA (i.e., ssDNA) to be sequenced and a short DNA primer.
A ring-shaped protein (nanopore) through which ssDNA would travel.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.10.2): polymerase-based sequencing needs ssDNA template, primer, four fluorescent nucleotides, sensors and software. The nanopore is the alternative method.

questions.stem: The steps of Shotgun genome sequencing are listed below. Which of them is step 2 from the beginning?

options.text: Isolate the bacterium to a pure culture.
Clone the DNA fragments using a plasmid cloning vector.
Sequence the cloned DNA fragment and get its nucleotide sequence.
Extract DNA and fragment it by cutting with a restriction endonuclease.
Use a computer to align the nucleotide sequences to get the full genome sequence.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (shotgun slide / Fig. 6.25): isolate the organism (1), extract DNA and partially digest it with a restriction enzyme (2), clone fragments (3), sequence (4), align by software (5).

sections.heading: Use of cloned DNA: DNA fingerprinting

questions.stem: Which of these allows DNA fingerprinting by restriction fragment-length polymorphism (RFLP) to identify different individuals of the same species?

options.text: Random mutation in the genome of different individuals of the same species.
The difference in the size of the genomes of different individuals of the same species.
Random mutations in the genome that affect some restriction endonuclease digestion sites.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.10.3, Fig. 6.26A): RFLP depends on point mutations that destroy restriction-enzyme recognition sites, changing fragment sizes.

sections.heading: Use of cloned DNA: Transgenesis, DNA vaccine, and edible vaccines

questions.stem: Which of the following is a transgenic organism and a GMO or LMO?

options.text: A twig of a Gala apple tree grafted to the stem of a crabapple tree.
A mule born to a mare mother and a donkey father.
A baby born to an artificially inseminated woman.
A rice plant carrying a gene from a carrot plant.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.10.5): transgenesis = a gene of one species placed in another's chromosomes; a rice plant carrying a carrot gene is transgenic. Grafting, mule and artificial insemination are not. Confirmed correct on your OLQ 6 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Edible vaccines are vaccines integrated into food substances. Which of these serves as the true vaccine in an edible vaccine?

options.text: The glycoprotein gene of a pathogenic virus inserted into the chromosome of a strawberry plant.
Strawberries of a plant transgenic for the viral glycoprotein gene.
Viral glycoprotein expressed in the strawberries.
The glycoprotein gene of a pathogenic virus.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.10.5): vaccines are microbial proteins; an edible vaccine delivers the viral protein produced in the plant, so the expressed glycoprotein is the true vaccine. Confirmed correct on your OLQ 6 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Why are DNA vaccines not administered in humans?

options.text: DNA may be inserted into the human genome, leading to harmful mutations.
All needed vaccines for human diseases are available in traditional form.
DNA vaccines work only in animals, not in human cells.
DNA vaccination is excessively painful.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.10.6): DNA vaccines are discouraged because foreign DNA can insert into a human chromosome, causing mutations and tumors.
