questions.stem: Which of the following is the definition of bioinformatics?

options.text: Sequencing genomes of microorganisms.
Identifying the mRNAs expressed by a tumor cell.
Application of computers to the interpretation of biological data.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.12): bioinformatics = application of computers to the collection, organization, analysis and sharing of biological data.

questions.stem: You want to find out the nucleotide sequence of an mRNA of a gene of Helicobacter pylori. Which of the following databases should you investigate?

options.text: TIGR.
PubMed.
GenBank.
Swissprot.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.12): GenBank/EMBL are the gene sequence databases, Swissprot is protein, TIGR is the complete genome database, PubMed is literature. A single gene's nucleotide sequence -> GenBank. Confirmed correct on your OLQ 6 attempt 1 (19/20).

questions.stem: Which of the following ethical problems regarding biotechnology is far-fetched as of today?

options.text: Unforeseen effects of gene therapy.
Manipulation of the germline human genome.
Leakage or trading of personal genetic information.
Restoration of extinct species through cloning and hybridization.
Severe food allergy and inflammatory bowel disease from GM food crops.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.11): unforeseen gene-therapy effects, human genome editing, genetic privacy and GM-food allergy/IBD are all discussed as real concerns; restoring extinct species is not mentioned. CONFIRMED BY ELIMINATION on your OLQ 6 attempt: you picked E and Canvas marked it wrong. A (gene-therapy effects), B (germline manipulation) and C (genetic privacy) are all concerns his chapter lists as real, so D, restoration of extinct species, is the one left as far-fetched.

questions.stem: Which of the following suspicions on GM/LM organisms have been found to be a significant proven reality as of today?

options.text: Dissemination of GMO super pests in nature.
Dissemination of GMO superweeds in nature.
Fatal health effects of GMO grains and vegetables.
Market monopoly and market manipulation by biotech companies.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§6.11): superweeds and super pests 'have not been observed', and the fatal health effects of GM food have not been shown, whereas farmers have actually lost lawsuits to biotech companies over seed patents - the monopoly is real. The earlier key answered superweeds, which the text says have NOT been observed. Confirmed correct on your OLQ 6 attempt 1 (19/20).

chapters.title: How to Grow and Control Microbial Growth

questions.stem: Which of the following sentences best expresses the reality of the growth of a unicellular microbe?

options.text: A daughter bacterial cell becomes as large as the mother cell.
A thousand bacteria are generated from a single bacterium.
A bacterium produced an endospore.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Unicellular growth = growth in number, so 'a thousand bacteria generated from one' is the reality. A describes growth in size (which the text says does not really happen); C is spore formation, not growth. [PDF p.1 Part 1 intro: 'Subcellular and unicellular microbes grow by number but not by size, because the size of the parent and progeny is about the same.'] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 7 attempt 1 (18/20).

sections.heading: How microbes grow in the natural environment

questions.stem: All microbes are essentially __________ organisms because __________.

options.text: terrestrial/microbes may grow on semisolid media
aquatic/ about 70% of the volume of cytoplasm is water
terrestrial/microbial envelope is designed to resist desiccation
aquatic/microbes have few adaptations to live in dry environments

questions.answerRationale: Course text: The chapter's stated reason for 'aquatic' is that microbes quickly desiccate in dry/terrestrial settings, i.e. few adaptations to dry environments (D). The '70% of cytoplasm is water' reason in B appears nowhere in the chapter; the old key used a general-textbook fact instead of the professor's own reason. [7.1: 'Almost all microbes can be considered aquatic organisms because they quickly desiccate in open terrestrial environments and are damaged by UV radiation.' Slide: 'All microbes are essentially aquatic'.] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 7 attempt 1 (18/20).

questions.stem: Which of the following may not harm microbial growth in natural environments?

options.text: Acid rain or alkaline factory runoff.
Water completely fills the air capillaries of the soil.
Excessive microbial species diversity in one environment.
Presence of excess heavy metals and synthetic chemicals in the soil.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: A (acid/alkaline runoff) and D (heavy metals/synthetic chemicals) are pollution, B is waterlogging - all stated to harm microbial life. Species diversity is the normal community state, not a harm. [7.1 Soil: 'Excess water floods the air capillaries of soil and drastically reduces biodiversity. Polluted soil and water are also poor in biodiversity.']

questions.stem: Although there are millions of bacterial species, only about 6,000 have been identified and named so far. Which of the following is the most plausible reason?

options.text: Most bacteria that live in the environment are inaccessible to microbiologists.
Most bacteria are harmless and thus not interesting to microbiologists.
Most bacterial species cannot be grown in the laboratory media.
Most bacteria live inside the cells of other organisms.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Instructor-marked answer C, matching the chapter text. [7.2.2 Biological factors: 'The interdependence is so intense that most microbes (>99%) cannot be grown in the laboratory.']

questions.stem: Which of the following bacterial infections will be most difficult to treat?

options.text: Bacteria growing in the blood.
Bacteria growing on the mucous membrane.
Bacteria growing inside the lung, forming a biofilm.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Biofilms protect bacteria from antimicrobials and host defenses, so a lung biofilm is hardest to treat; the chapter also notes organic substances protect microbes from treatment agents (7.7). Confirmed correct on your OLQ 7 attempt 1 (18/20).

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most suitable substratum for pathogenic bacteria (in the human body) to form a biofilm?

options.text: An IUD or a pacemaker.
The inner wall of a vein or an artery.
The surfaces of the heart and the heart valves.
The surface of the trachea, bronchioles, or alveoli.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: The chapter names implanted inanimate devices as the biofilm substratum; an IUD or pacemaker matches exactly. [7.1: 'Bloodborne bacteria may also form biofilms on inanimate substances in the body, such as pacemakers and venous catheters.'] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 7 attempt 1 (18/20).

questions.stem: Which of these may contain viral pathogens that can cause respiratory infections?

options.text: Conditioned air coming out from room ducts.
Air released by cooling tower of an electric plant.
Air of a office room where five people are sit for six hours.
Air released by a modern incinerator for burning solid waste including animal carcass.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Respiratory viruses come from people breathing/sneezing, so an occupied office room's air is the source. [7.1 Air: 'Humans and animals release microbes through breathing and sneezing as droplets... The droplets may stay airborne for a few minutes to a few hours... Contaminated air is the primary source of respiratory infections.' Airborne vi...] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 7 attempt 1 (18/20).

questions.stem: Optimum growth temperatures of some microbes are shown below. Which of the microbes is a psychrotroph?

options.text: 15 degrees C.
25 degrees C.
37 degrees C.
52 degrees C.
72 degrees C.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Table 7.1 gives the psychrotroph optimum as 25 C (psychrophile 10, mesophile 37, thermophile 65, hyperthermophile 90). [Table 7.1: Psychrotrophs range 0 to 35, optimum 25 C.]

questions.stem: The range and optimum temperatures for growth of mesophiles are _________, respectively.

options.text: 0-30 degrees C and 25 degrees C
10-50 degrees C and 30 degrees C
30-65 degrees C and 50 degrees C
15-42 degrees C and 37 degrees C

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Stated directly in Table 7.1. [Table 7.1: Mesophiles 15 to 42, optimum 37.] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 7 attempt 1 (18/20).

questions.stem: Which of the following solutions will cause a bacterium (Pseudomonas aeruginosa) to suffer plasmolysis?

options.text: Seawater (contains 3.5% salt).
Freshwater (contains <0.05% salt).
Blood plasma (295 milliosmole/kg).
Normal saline solution (contains 0.9% salt).

questions.answerRationale: Course text: C and D are the optimal 0.9%/295 mOsm; freshwater is survivable thanks to the cell wall; 3.5% seawater is at the brine level that causes plasmolysis in a non-halophile like P. aeruginosa. [7.2.2 Osmotic pressure: body fluids ~0.9% (295 mOsm/kg) optimal; 'A few bacterial pathogens, such as the genera Vibrio and Escherichia, survive in brackish water (0.5-3%). questions.stem: An obligate anaerobe such as Clostridium perfringens must ________ to survive in the bottom mud of a pond.

options.text: remove free radicals and detoxify reactive oxygen species
ferment or conduct anaerobic respiration to obtain ATP
form endospores
produce biofilm Chemical and biological factors of microbial growth

questions.answerRationale: Course text: In anoxic mud the anaerobe must get ATP without oxygen (fermentation/anaerobic respiration). A is what aerobes need; endospores are a dormancy strategy, not how it lives/grows there. (Option D carries a garbled section header 'Chemical and biological factors of microbial growth'.) [7.2.2 Oxygen: 'Obligate anaerobes (such as the genera Actinomyces, Clostridium...) and obligate fermenters ... thrive by fermenting.'] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 7 attempt 1 (18/20).

questions.stem: Why do aerobes need enzymes such as SOD, catalase, and oxidase?

options.text: To convert CO2 to O2.
To convert O2 to CO2.
To detoxify reactive oxygen species (ROS).
To harvest oxygen and to increase the rate of respiration.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Stated directly. (Stem says 'oxidase'; the chapter says peroxidase - wording slip, does not change the answer.) [7.2.2: 'The enzymes that detoxify the reactive chemicals include superoxide dismutase (SOD), catalase, and peroxidase.'] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 7 attempt 1 (18/20).

questions.stem: Which of the following chemical reactions does the enzyme SOD catalyze?

options.text: H2O2 + NADH + H+ ® 2H2O +NAD+

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Instructor-marked B matches the reaction printed in the chapter. TEXT ERROR: the chapter sentence says SOD neutralizes 'singlet oxygen', but the reaction (and the slide) is on superoxide O2-; singlet oxygen is 1O2. [7.2.2: 'SOD neutralizes singlet oxygen by the reaction 2O2- + 2H+ -> H2O2 + O2'; slide: 'Superoxide (O2-), effect of SOD'.]

questions.stem: A bacterium uses oxygen as the terminal electron acceptor, but lacks SOD and peroxidase. The bacterium is most likely a ________.

options.text: microaerophile
obligatory aerobe
obligate anaerobe
facultative anaerobe
aerotolerant anaerobe

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Matches the chapter's definition of a microaerophile word for word. [7.2.2: 'Some pathogens (such as Helicobacter pylori and Neisseria gonorrhoeae) require oxygen for respiration but lack an enzyme to detoxify the free radicals. questions.stem: All the following are reactive oxygen species (ROS). Which of them is the singlet oxygen?

options.text: O3
OH.
H2O2

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Singlet oxygen is written 1O2 in the chapter. [7.2.2: 'superoxide (O2-), hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), and singlet oxygen (1O2)'.] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 7 attempt 1 (18/20).

questions.stem: Which of the following bacteria, by definition, is an obligate halophile?

options.text: It does not grow in the presence of NaCl.
It needs NaCl in the medium to grow.
It tolerates a low concentration of NaCl but not a high concentration of NaCl.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: 'Obligate' halophile = requires salt (NaCl) to grow. C describes a halotolerant organism. [7.2.2: brine inhibits most microbes 'except obligate halophiles (salt-loving bacteria and archaea)'.]

questions.stem: Some sulfur bacteria survive in acid pools near copper mines. These bacteria are _________, and their enzymes must function well at the pH_______.

options.text: acidophile/ 2-4
acidophile/ 6-7
alkaliphile/8-10

questions.stem: The main sources of nutrients of pathogenic bacteria (living in the human body) are shown below. One of the sources is incorrect. The item is ___________.

options.text: carbon: Organic molecules from live or dead cells
nitrogen: N2 gas and dissolved nitrate salts
phosphorus: nucleic acids
trace elements: water
sulfur: amino acids Aseptic techniques and growth media

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Pathogens in the human body get nitrogen from organic molecules (amino acids, nucleotides), not from N2 gas (nitrogen fixation is a soil-bacteria trait) or nitrate. questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the routine laboratory septic techniques?

options.text: Keep culture media sterile.
Protect laboratory workers from infections.
Dispose of the biohazard wastes in a septic tank.
Prevent contamination of the microbial culture media.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: A, B and D are items (a), (d) and (e). Dumping biohazard waste in a septic tank is not appropriate disposal. [7.3 Standard aseptic techniques (a)-(f): medium kept sterile; microbes from workspace must not enter workers; cultures protected from contamination; 'biohazard wastes ... must be appropriately disposed of'. questions.stem: Which of the following is an advantage of the semisolid culture media?

options.text: The media is formed in plates or tubes.
Can be scaled up to grow a large batch of microbes.
Many but not all microbes grow on semisolid media.
Establishing a pure culture or growing microbes that need a substratum.

[7.3 Broth vs semisolid: 'Broth is used for large-scale microbial culture. However, separating cellular microbes requires a semisolid medium.'] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 7 attempt 1 (18/20).

questions.stem: A medium has water, glucose, NaCl, MgSO4, K2HPO4, KH2PO4, agar, and tap water. The medium is a ________ medium.

options.text: defined broth
defined semisolid
complex semisolid
selective semisolid

WHY NOT 100%: if the professor just meant ordinary water, B is the answer. [7.3: 'A chemically defined medium contains pure chemical compounds ... of known chemical composition'; 'A complex medium contains ... complex nutrients of unknown chemical composition, such as peptone, tryptone, and yeast extract.' Semis...] SECOND CHECK (his slides, OpenStax, Exam 2 study guide): No source mentions tap water in a medium. The slide's 'water and pure chemical (formula known)' makes tap water (impure, unknown composition) the likely planted trap -> C. But the MMAHP definition ties 'complex' to complex NUTRIENTS (peptone, yeast extract), which tap water is not -> B defensible. OUTSIDE REVIEW (two other AI reviewers, 2026-10-12): one agreed with C, one chose B (defined semisolid), reasoning that typical intro questions would not treat "tap water" as making a medium complex. differential medium
enrichment medium
selective-differential medium Growing bacteria and bacterial growth curve

options.text: low oxygen and high nitrogen concentration
higher CO2 and lower oxygen level
high moisture

questions.stem: Which of the following is the stationary phase of a bacterial growth curve?

options.text: In this phase, the death rate is high, and the growth rate is low.
In this phase, the death and growth rates are nearly identical.
In this phase, the death rate is negligible, the growth rate is fixed and high.
In this phase, the death rate is negligible, and the growth rate is negligible or very low.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Instructor-marked B, matching the text. [7.4: 'At some point, the rate of cell growth equals the rate of cell death. This phase is known as the stationary phase.']

log/stationary
stationary/declining

options.text: Nothing, it is impossible in a closed system.
The scientist should grow the bacterium in a small pond.
The scientists should oxygenate the culture by bubbling filtered air.
The scientist should remove some culture and replenish the volume with a fresh medium.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: D paraphrases the chapter's method. (Stem is garbled: 'indefinitelshould y. What the scientists do' = 'indefinitely. What should the scientist do'.) questions.stem: A scientist serially diluted a stool sample of a diarrhea patient in this manner: (i) Stock sample, (ii) 1 ml of stock sample+ 9 ml of LB broth, mixed; (iii) 1 ml of diluted sample ii + 9 ml of LB broth, mixed; (iv) 1 ml of diluted sample iii+ 9 ml of LB broth, mixed; (v) 1 ml of diluted sample iv+ 9 ml of LB broth, mixed. questions.answerRationale: Course text: Working: ii = 1/10, iii = 1/100, iv = 1/1,000, v = 1/10,000. In this chapter the 0.1 ml plating volume is handled by the separate x10, not folded into df, so df = 1/10,000. The instructor-marked q29 (sample iv -> '34 x 10 x 1,000') confirms this convention. Note: had the plating volume been folded in, the answer would be 1/100,000 (D). [7.6: 'N = n x 10 x dilution factor ... 10 is to compensate for the 0.1 ml sample used for plating'; worked example 'diluted 10,000-fold'.] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 7 attempt 1 (18/20).

questions.stem: A scientist serially diluted a stool sample of a diarrhea patient in this manner: (i) Stock sample, (ii) 1 ml of stock sample + 9 ml of LB broth, mixed; (iii) 1 ml of diluted sample ii + 9 ml of LB broth, mixed; (iv) 1 ml of diluted sample iii+ 9 ml of LB broth, mixed; (v) 1 ml of diluted sample iv+ 9 ml of LB broth, mixed. questions.answerRationale: Course text: Instructor-marked B. Working: iii (1/100) = 320 colonies, >300, rejected; v (1/10,000) = 5, <10, rejected; iv (1/1,000) = 34, usable -> N = 34 x 10 x 1,000 = 3.4 x 10^5 cfu/ml. [Fig 7.10 / 7.6: significant colony count = 10-300 colonies; N = n x 10 x df.]

questions.stem: A600 of an E. coli culture in LB broth was 0.5. The culture is currently at the _______ phase of the growth curve.

options.text: lag
log
stationary
declining

questions.stem: A 100 ml sample of pond water was filtered using a 0.4-micron filter paper, and the filter paper was exposed to a MacConkey agar plate. 120 bacterial colonies developed after overnight incubation of the plate. What is the bacterial count of the pond water, and what type of bacteria were counted by the protocol?

120 cfu/ ml, all types of bacteria present in the pond water.
1,200 cfu/ml, G(-) bacteria present in the pond water.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Working: 120 cfu / 100 ml = 1.20 cfu/ml. questions.stem: A person treated a surgical knife with 10% Clorox® solution. She performed _______.

options.text: sanitizing
sterilization
disinfection
pasteurization
antisepsis

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Chemical treatment of an inanimate object with dilute bleach is disinfection (ILD), not sterilization (no endospore claim). Sanitizing is defined as LLD of cooking pots/utensils; antisepsis is for skin; pasteurization is physical. [Table 7.4: 'Disinfection - Elimination of microbes from inanimate objects'; 7.11: 'A 10% Clorox solution may effectively inactivate all viruses and bacterial cells in a few minutes'; Table 7.6 lists chlorine under ILD.] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 7 attempt 1 (18/20).

questions.stem: Pasteurization is technically comparable to which of these?

options.text: HLD.
ILD.
LLD.
UHLD.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Instructor-marked B; the two definitions line up exactly. [Table 7.4: ILD 'Removing all vegetative cells and viruses from an inanimate object'; 7.10.1: heat pasteurization 'inactivates viruses and vegetative cells but not bacterial endospores'.]

questions.stem: Which of the following definitions is CORRECT?

options.text: Commercial Sterilization: Sufficient treatment to inactivate Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
Degerming: Mechanical removal of microbes from the surface of live tissues.
Disinfection: Removal of vegetative pathogens from skin surfaces.
Antisepsis: Removal of pathogens from surfaces of utensils.
Sterilization: Removal of all vegetative cells.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Degerming is antisepsis (live tissue), done by mechanical or chemical means - B fits the slide. A ('commercial sterilization') is not defined in the chapter and TB-level killing is ILD; C/D swap disinfection (inanimate) and antisepsis (skin); E sterilization removes ALL microbes, not just vegetative cells. Re-checked against his slide 22, 'Definition of the commonly used terms': "Degerming - low level antisepsis by mechanical/chemical means". His slide defines disinfection as elimination of microbes on inanimate surfaces and sterilization as freeing an object of ALL live microbes, which rules out C, D and E; OpenStax ties commercial sterilization to C. botulinum, which rules out A. B. Confirmed correct on your OLQ 7 attempt 1 (18/20).

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is technically correct?

options.text: The higher the number of microbes, the faster the killing.
The higher the amount of biofilm, the faster the rate of killing.
When Mycobacterium and naked viruses are inactivated, the surface is completely disinfected.
High-intensity treatment with a short exposure time is equivalent to low-intensity treatment with a long exposure time.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: D is the chapter's sentence. A and B are reversed; C fails because endospores, cysts and prions are more resilient than Mycobacterium/naked viruses. [7.7: 'In general, a short exposure at a high intensity is equivalent to a longer exposure at a lower intensity.' Also 'The higher the concentration of microbes, the longer the treatment must last'; organic substances protect microbes.] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 7 attempt 1 (18/20).

questions.stem: The membrane, proteins, and DNA are the major targets for inactivating microbes. If you destroy the plasma membrane of a cellular microbe, which of the following aspects will be immediately affected?

options.text: All metabolic activities will collapse.
Biological homeostasis will collapse.
Protein synthesis and processing will collapse.
Energy (ATP) synthesis/acquisition will collapse.
Genome replication and transcription will collapse.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: The plasma membrane is the barrier that maintains the cell's internal environment, so its destruction immediately collapses homeostasis (leakage of contents, loss of gradients); the other processes fail as consequences. Confirmed correct on your OLQ 7 attempt 1 (18/20).

questions.stem: Which of the following is a valid definition of D value?

options.text: Time of heat treatment needed to reduce the number of microbes of a sample by one log.
Intensity of treatment needed to reduce the number of microbes of a sample by 90%.
Reduction of the number of microbes of a sample to ~10 to the power 0 (i.e., 1)
Two of these definitions are valid.
All these definitions are valid.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Instructor-marked D. A (one-log reduction time) and B (90% reduction) are the two valid definitions; C is not a D value. Thus, each D value reduces the microbial count by one log.']

questions.stem: After one D-value of treatment, the bacterial count in a batch of soup was 100,000/liter. What would be the bacterial count after three more D-value equivalents of treatment?

options.text: 1,000/liter.
100/liter.
10/liter.
0/liter.

questions.answerRationale: Course text: Working: 100,000 = 10^5; three more D values -> 10^4, 10^3, 10^2 = 100/liter. [7.7: 'each D value reduces the microbial count by one log'.] Confirmed correct on your OLQ 7 attempt 1 (18/20).

questions.stem: A stainless-steel dental probe to be used in cleaning teeth should be treated with ___________ and an endoscope (made of plastic tubing) should receive a _________.

options.text: HLD/ILD
ILD/LLD
HLD/LLD
Autoclaving/HLD

questions.answerRationale: Course text: A heat-durable steel probe that contacts gums/blood gets sterilized (autoclaved); the chapter names endoscopes as the HLD example. questions.stem: In theory, a tongue depressor is considered a __________ item, and a dental probe used for teeth cleaning is considered a __________ item.

options.text: critical/ semi-critical
semi-critical/ critical
non-critical/non-critical
non-critical/ semi-critical

[7.7 Risk of infection (Spaulding): 'items such as the oral spatula that touch intact mucous membranes are semi-critical; and items such as needles and venous catheters that touch sterile tissue and blood are critical.']

questions.stem: If you have killed/inactivated ___________, you might have killed/inactivated the rest of the microbes shown here.

options.text: bacterial or fungal spores
enveloped viruses
protozoan cysts
fungal hyphae
naked viruses Hand washing

options.text: touching infants
preparing food and examining patients
waking up from sleep and using restrooms
touching garbage, animals, animal food, and animal waste

Rinse hands after lathering.
Take soap before wetting hands.
Use a filter-free forced-air hand drier.
Lather hands thoroughly for 10 seconds.

its ingredients include polyacrylate
one’s hands are visibly dirty

Remove the environmental microbes but not the resident microbes on hand.
Remove the environmental microbes and the resident microbes that may readily shed from the hands.

questions.stem: For what reasons is dry heat sterilization sometimes preferred to moist heat sterilization (i.e., autoclaving)?

options.text: Dry heat is faster and more efficient.
Dry heat is less expensive and thus more affordable.

A synthetic peptide that mimics the spike protein and binds the ACE2 protein.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a good attribute of nucleotide analogs as antiviral drugs?

options.text: Nucleotide analogs make the newly synthesized DNA or RNA highly fragile.
Nucleotide analogs increase the rate of mutation in the virus genomes.
Nucleotide analogs interfere with DNA or RNA replication.
Nucleotide analogs rapidly kill susceptible host cells.

questions.answerRationale: Rapidly killing the host cells a drug is meant to protect is a toxicity liability, not a desirable feature - unlike genome fragility, increased mutation rate, and interference with replication, which are all the drug's intended antiviral mechanisms.

questions.stem: Highly active antiretroviral therapy (HART) combines two or more antiviral drugs, and the therapy is highly effective. Which of the following is NOT a good reason for adopting combination antiviral therapy?

options.text: Multiple drugs in the mixture inhibit multiple drug targets of the virus.
The drug mixture prevents rapid mutation and evolution of the virus.
The drug cocktail prevents the development of viral drug resistance.
The toxicity of the combined drugs acts synergistically.

questions.answerRationale: Synergistic toxicity (more combined harm) is a downside, not a reason to combine drugs - unlike hitting multiple targets, slowing viral evolution, and preventing resistance, which are the actual, desirable justifications for combination therapy.

questions.stem: Which of the following steps of the influenza virus replication cycle is inhibited by zanamivir?

Budding of the virus particles out of the plasma membrane.
Separation of the egressed viruses from the plasma membrane of the progenitor cells.
Assembly of viral envelope glycoproteins and matrix proteins on the plasma membrane of the host cell.

questions.answerRationale: Zanamivir inhibits neuraminidase, the enzyme that cleaves sialic acid to let newly budded virus particles detach from the infected cell surface - without it, progeny viruses stay stuck to the cell.

questions.stem: Which of the following cells has the most optimal conditions to establish an antiviral state?

options.text: A cell that has secreted interferons.
A cell that has been infected by a virus.
A cell has expressed receptors for interferons.
A cell that has its interferon receptors bound to secreted interferons.

questions.answerRationale: The antiviral state is established once a cell's interferon receptors are actually bound by secreted interferon, triggering the downstream defensive gene expression - simply secreting interferon or expressing unbound receptors doesn't by itself establish the state.

questions.stem: A cell that has established an antiviral state. Which of these is not an expected activity of the cell?

options.text: Preventing transcription of viral genes or translation of viral proteins.
Replicating chromosomes and dividing by mitosis.
Destroying/modifying viral RNA and proteins.
Preventing entry or egress of the virus.
Preventing virus assembly.

questions.answerRationale: A cell mounting a defensive antiviral response generally shuts down normal macromolecular synthesis and growth to limit resources available to the virus - continuing to divide by mitosis as usual is not part of that defensive posture.

questions.stem: The following statements describe how interfering dsRNA inhibits the translation of viral mRNAs. One of the statements is INCORRECT. Which of the statements is that?

options.text: Dicer cuts the interfering dsRNA into small pieces about 25 bp.
RISC takes the 25 bp RNA fragments to use them as guide RNAs.
RISC hybridizes a guide RNA with the target mRNA of the virus.
Dicer cuts the viral mRNA that is hybridized with the guide RNA.
Ribosomes fail to translate the fragmented viral mRNA (the mRNA disintegrates).

questions.answerRationale: Dicer's job is only to chop the initial dsRNA into small guide fragments; the actual cleavage of the target viral mRNA (once paired with the guide strand inside RISC) is carried out by Argonaute's slicer activity, not by Dicer again.

questions.stem: RNA interference (RNAi) drugs have been approved for treating certain diseases. Which of the following is the most pressing problem of RNAi therapy?

Healthy cells receiving the dsRNA (i.e., synthesis of excess interferons).
Delivery of dsRNA inside the target cells in the specific tissues of specific organs.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most suitable target for developing antibacterial chemotherapeutic agents?

options.text: Lipid synthesis and membrane dynamics.
Cell wall synthesis and maintenance.
DNA replication and recombination.
RNA transcription and processing.
Protein synthesis and processing.

questions.answerRationale: The bacterial cell wall is the gold-standard example of selective toxicity, since human cells have no cell wall at all - making it the safest, most bacteria-specific drug target of the options listed.

questions.stem: Why bacterial DNA replication is not an ideal target for developing antibacterial drugs.

options.text: No known agent inhibits bacterial DNA polymerase.

Agents that inhibit bacterial DNA replication cannot penetrate the bacterial cell wall.

questions.stem: Why are membrane-active antibiotics such as polymyxins, daptomycin, and gramicidin usually used in treating surface wounds and not as orally and parenterally (injected) administered drugs? Note: Only the best answer will be scored.

options.text: The drugs are not absorbed if taken orally or injected.

The drugs are made of a polypeptide and a lipid.

Attachment of NAG-NAM disaccharide to an existing polysaccharide.
Cross-linking of two amino acids of the oligopeptides of two NAM entities.
Transport of NAG-NAM disaccharide units outside of the plasma membrane.

Clavulanate reduces the toxicity of amoxicillin.
Clavulanate increases the bioavailability of amoxicillin.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§8.2.2): clavulanate, sulbactam and tazobactam bind and inhibit beta-lactamases, so the penicillin survives (amoxicillin-clavulanate = Augmentin).

questions.stem: A strain of Staphylococcus aureus became resistant to methicillin because it produces a beta-lactamase enzyme. How does the beta-lactamase enzyme make the bacterium methicillin-resistant?

options.text: The enzyme cuts open the thiazolidine ring of methicillin.
The enzyme cuts C-N bond and opens the beta-lactam ring of methicillin.
The enzyme binds methicillin and prevents transpeptidases from binding the antibiotics.
The enzyme chemically modifies methicillin by attaching a methyl group to the beta-lactamase ring.

questions.answerRationale: Beta-lactamase enzymes work by hydrolyzing the C-N bond within the beta-lactam ring itself, destroying the ring's ability to bind and inhibit penicillin-binding proteins.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a purpose of designing semi-synthetic or fully synthetic antibiotics?

options.text: Reduce drug toxicity.
Reduce drug bioavailability.
Making the drugs broad-spectrum.
Making the drugs resistant to bacterial enzymes.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§8.2.2): newer drugs have improved spectrum, efficacy and bioavailability and resist beta-lactamases. Designers raise bioavailability, never reduce it.

questions.stem: Which of the following antibiotics can be used in treating Mycoplasma pneumoniae?

options.text: Cephalosporins or cephamycins (3rd, 4th or 5th generation).
Aminopenicillins such as carbenicillin.
Monobactams such as meropenem.
Fully synthetic carbapenems.
None of these antibiotics.

questions.answerRationale: Mycoplasma pneumoniae has no cell wall at all, so every option listed here (cephalosporins, aminopenicillins, monobactams, carbapenems) - all beta-lactam, cell-wall-targeting drugs - has no target to act on and is completely ineffective.

sections.heading: Other inhibitors of cell wall synthesis

questions.stem: Which of these statements about vancomycin is INCORRECT?

options.text: It is made of amino acids and sugars.
It is only effective against G(+) bacteria.
It is effective against MERSA and VERSA.
It prevents the crosslinking of oligopeptides of the bacterial cell wall.
It is effective against the naturally drug-resistant soil bacterium Clostridium difficile.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§8.2.2): vancomycin is effective only against some G(+) bacteria, including MRSA and susceptible C. difficile; VRSA is by definition vancomycin-resistant. OLQ 8 Q4 also treats VRSA as needing linezolid, not vancomycin. Confirmed correct on your second graded OLQ 8 attempt (19.5/20).

questions.stem: Ethambutol inhibits arabinogalactan synthesis. Which of the bacteria should the drug be effective against?

options.text: G(+) bacteria such as actinobacteria.
G(-) bacteria such as proteobacteria.
G(-) bacteria such as mycoplasmas.
Spirochetes.

questions.answerRationale: Arabinogalactan is a component specifically of the mycobacterial (Actinobacteria) cell wall, so a drug targeting its synthesis is effective against that group specifically.

questions.stem: Cycloserine is related to a/an________, and it is used as a second line of antibiotics to treat__________ if other antibiotics do not work.

options.text: fatty acid/ anaerobic bacterial infections of soft tissues
amino acid/multidrug-resistant mycobacteria
nucleotide/ disseminated bacterial infections
monosaccharide/ mixed bacterial infections Inhibitors of DNA replication

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§8.2.2): cycloserine blocks D-alanine-D-alanine ligase and alanine racemase (a D-alanine, i.e. amino acid, analog) and is a second-line drug for tuberculosis when other treatments cannot be used.

questions.stem: How do fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA replication in bacteria?

options.text: They inhibit bacterial helicase.
They inhibit bacterial DNA polymerase.
They inhibit bacterial DNA topoisomerase.
They inhibit the bacterial DNA sliding clamp.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§8.2.3): fluoroquinolones bind DNA gyrase / topoisomerase IV of bacteria.

questions.stem: Metronidazole binds to DNA and causes single-stranded DNA breaks. Why is this a medical concern, and why is the drug effective only against anaerobic bacteria and protozoa?

options.text: The drug may create drug-resistant bacteria; aerobes do not absorb the drug.
A high dose of the drug is necessary to make the drug effective; oxygen destroys the drug.
The drug may mutate the host cell’s chromosomes; only anaerobes have nitroreductase to activate the drug.

questions.answerRationale: Metronidazole is a prodrug that must be activated by nitroreductase, an enzyme found specifically in anaerobic organisms - explaining both its anaerobe-only selectivity and the genotoxicity concern once the activated form damages DNA.

questions.stem: Clofazimine, one of the most effective drugs to treat leprosy, binds guanine residues. Which of these bacterial activities does the drug directly affect?

options.text: Lipid synthesis
DNA replication.
RNA transcription.
Protein synthesis and processing.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§8.2.3 and the nucleic-acid slide): clofazimine binds guanine residues of DNA and 'most likely inhibits DNA replication'. The earlier key answered RNA transcription from outside knowledge; the course never says that.

questions.stem: Mutations in which of these genes would make a bacterium resistant to rifamycin, and why is rifamycin always used in combination therapy?

options.text: The DNA polymerase gene; the drug is highly toxic.
The DNA helicase gene, the drug is unstable if used alone.
The RNA polymerase gene; bacteria readily become resistant to the drug.

questions.answerRationale: Rifamycin targets bacterial RNA polymerase directly, so mutations in that gene's sequence confer resistance; bacteria are also well known to develop rifamycin resistance quickly when it is used alone, which is why it is never given as monotherapy.

questions.stem: Aminoglycosides bind the 23S rRNA of the 30S ribosome particles. Which of the following steps of protein synthesis do aminoglycosides most likely inhibit?

options.text: Translation initiation.
Translation elongation.
Translation termination.
Post-termination event (such as ribosome recycling).

questions.answerRationale: Fig. 8.14 of the chapter places aminoglycosides (with aminocyclitols and tetracyclines) at '30S / initiation'. The earlier key answered elongation from the text line about error-prone elongation; OLQ 8 marked elongation wrong, and the figure settles it.

questions.stem: (a) Which of the following aminoglycosides is nontoxic, and (b) which of the aminoglycosides is used in treating/preventing Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections of the lung of cystic fibrosis patients?

options.text: (a) Kanamycin/(b) Neomycin.
(a) Neomycin/ (b) Streptomycin.
(a) Streptomycin/ (b) gentamycin.
(a) Streptomycin/ (b) Plazomicin.
(a) None of the aminoglycosides/ (b) Tobramycin.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§8.2.5): all aminoglycosides are moderately or severely nephrotoxic and neurotoxic (none is nontoxic); tobramycin is the inhalation mist used for Pseudomonas in cystic fibrosis.

sections.heading: Inhibitors of protein synthesis: Tetracyclines and macrolides

questions.stem: All tetracyclines have a __________ structure, and of the tetracyclines, __________ is often used in treating sexually transmitted and intracellular bacterial pathogens.

options.text: polyketide/ doxycycline
macrocyclic ring/ minocycline
cyclobutene ring/ chlortetracycline

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§8.2.5): tetracyclines have a characteristic polyketide structure, and doxycycline is the most used for intracellular bacteria and bacterial STIs.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about tetracycline is INCORRECT?

options.text: Tetracyclines are narrow-spectrum antibiotics.
Tetracyclines become more toxic after the expiration date.
Tetracyclines deposit in the bones and can be teratogenic to fetuses.
The drugs bind 16S RNA of 30S ribosome, but they probably also bind 50S ribosomes.
Some tetracyclines are used in treating autoimmune diseases (the drugs are immunosuppressive)

questions.answerRationale: Tetracyclines are actually well-known broad-spectrum antibiotics, active against a wide range of Gram-positive, Gram-negative, and atypical organisms - calling them narrow-spectrum is the false statement here.

questions.stem: Macrolides, such as azithromycin, bind 23S rRNA, thus they bind _________ and prevent bacterial translation elongation.

options.text: 30S ribosomes
40S ribosomes
50S ribosomes Inhibitors of protein synthesis: other protein synthesis inhibiting antibiotics

questions.answerRationale: 23S rRNA is a structural component of the large (50S) ribosomal subunit, not the 30S or a eukaryotic 40S subunit.

questions.stem: To treat MERSA and VERSA infections, one would prefer ___________; and to treat bacterial meningitis, one would prefer _________.

options.text: oxazolidines (such as linezolid)/ chloramphenicol
chloramphenicol/ lincosamides (such as clindamycin)
lincosamides (such as clindamycin)/ streptogramins such as Synercid Inhibitors of folate synthesis

questions.answerRationale: Oxazolidinones like linezolid are a go-to choice against resistant Gram-positives like MRSA/VRSA, and chloramphenicol's well-known ability to cross the blood-brain barrier makes it a classic choice for bacterial meningitis.

questions.stem: Folates are vitamins ______, and they are essential for the synthesis of _________.

options.text: A/ DNA
B6/ RNA
B12/ protein
B9/ nucleotides and some amino acids

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§8.2.6): folate is vitamin B9, needed for adenosine, guanosine and thymidine synthesis (nucleotides) and some amino acids.

questions.stem: Sulfa drugs are structural analogs of the cellular molecule____________, and they bind the enzyme ____________.

options.text: para-amino salicylic acid (PAS)/ dihydrofolate synthase
para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA) / dihydrofolate synthase
gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)/ dihydrofolate reductase
monosodium glutamate (MSG)/ gamma glutamyl transpeptidase

questions.answerRationale: Sulfonamides are structural analogs of PABA and competitively block the folate-synthesis enzyme pathway at the dihydropteroate/dihydrofolate synthesis step - trimethoprim, not sulfa drugs, is the one that targets dihydrofolate reductase specifically.

questions.stem: The commonly prescribed drug BactrimTM contains __________, while ________ are used in combination with rifampin to treat tuberculosis and leprosy.

options.text: Dapsone and PASER/ Sulfamethoxazole and chloroquine
sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim/ Dapsone or PASER
sulphathiazole and chloroquine/ trimethoprim and Dapsone

questions.answerRationale: BactrimTM is the well-known brand combining sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim; dapsone or PASER are the drugs paired with rifampin for treating leprosy and tuberculosis respectively.

questions.stem: Why are sulfa drugs and trimethoprim almost always used in combination to treat bacterial infections and as prophylaxis for pneumocystis pneumonia?

options.text: Because the two drugs inhibit two enzymes in the same metabolic pathway.
Because the two drugs are totally ineffective if used alone.
Because the two drugs act synergistically.
Because of two of these reasons.
Because of all these reasons.

questions.answerRationale: Sulfa drugs and trimethoprim block two sequential enzymes in the same folate-synthesis pathway, which is both why they act synergistically and why they're described as targeting the same pathway - both A and C describe the same underlying reality, making "two of these reasons" the accurate answer.

sections.heading: Prevention and cure of fungal infections

questions.stem: One would avoid _______ to avoid aflatoxin (a carcinogen), and _________ to avoid amatoxin (an inhibitors of RNA polymerase II).

options.text: uninspected nut and nut oil/ unidentified wild mushroom
bread made of infected rye/ contaminated dry fruits, grain, and pork
contaminated cereal grain/ partially rotted fruits, and contaminated fruit juice

questions.answerRationale: Aflatoxin classically contaminates uninspected nuts (Aspergillus flavus), and amatoxin is the toxin famously found in unidentified wild mushrooms like the death cap.

questions.stem: Of the antifungal therapeutic agents, __________ group inhibits fungal polysaccharide synthesis, and _______ inhibit ergosterol synthesis __________.

options.text: echinocandins/ allylamines
flucytosine/ griseofulvin
polyenes/ flucytosine
allylamines/ azoles
azole/polyenes

questions.answerRationale: Echinocandins inhibit beta-glucan synthase, blocking fungal cell-wall polysaccharide synthesis; allylamines like terbinafine block an earlier step of ergosterol biosynthesis (squalene epoxidase).

questions.stem: All these drugs inhibit ergosterol synthesis EXCEPT _______, it binds the ergosterol and disrupts fungal membranes.

options.text: terbinafine
fluconazole
voriconazole
ketokonazole
ampotericin B

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§8.3.1): polyenes such as amphotericin B BIND membrane ergosterol and form channels; azoles (flu-, vori-, ketoconazole) and allylamines (terbinafine) inhibit ergosterol synthesis.

questions.stem: Sordarin, an experimental drug based on a fungal metabolite. Why is the drug called a broad-spectrum antifungal drug?

options.text: Because it inhibits fungal protein synthesis
Because it is effective against yeast and mold forms of fungi
Because it is derived from a fungal metabolite, but it is an antifungal agent.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§8.3.1, Sordarin): 'In test tubes, these agents are broad-spectrum antifungal agents, effective against both yeast and mold forms.' Protein-synthesis inhibition is its mechanism, not why it is called broad-spectrum. The earlier key answered the mechanism and invented an eEF2 detail the course never gives.

questions.stem: Which of these lessons do antiprotozoal drugs give to drug developers?

options.text: Modern science has won the war on infectious diseases.
Traditional drugs should be considered for rational drug development.
Protozoan infections are a public health problem only in the least developed countries.
There are only a few antiprotozoal drugs developed because only a few people get infected by the agents.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§8.4.1 and the 'Problems with antiprotozoal agents' slide): traditional drugs (quinine, artemisinin) became mainstream antiprotozoals, and the slide lists 'traditional drugs' and 'more research necessary'. The other options contradict the text.

questions.stem: All these antibacterial or antifungal agents are used in treating some protozoan infections. Which of these inhibits the DNA replication of some protozoans?

options.text: Pentamidine, metronidazole, and quinolones.
Clindamycin, tetracycline, and doxycycline.
Macrolides such as azithromycin.
Trimethoprim and sulfonamide.
Azoles and amphotericin B.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§8.4.1): pentamidine and metronidazole bind and damage DNA, and quinolones bind DNA gyrase and prevent DNA replication.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is CORRECT about heavy metal (arsenic and antimony) organic compounds used in treating protozoan infections?

options.text: The metal ions in the drugs primarily act by inducing oxidative damage to the enzymes of the target parasites.
The drugs are used to treat amebiasis (gastroenteritis) and trichomoniasis (vaginosis).
Bismuth salicylate is an effective antiprotozoal drug.
The drugs have only modest side effects.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§8.4.1): the metal ions (arsenic, antimony) probably oxidize sulfhydryl groups, inhibiting enzymes, and may cause oxidative damage. They treat sleeping sickness and leishmaniasis (not amebiasis/trichomoniasis) and are highly toxic. Bismuth salicylate is not covered as an antiprotozoal. WHY NOT 100%: the text says the metal ions probably oxidize sulfhydryl groups and cause oxidative damage (A). But the antiprotozoal slide lists BISMUTH with arsenic and antimony as heavy-metal antiprotozoals, which could make C true; the stem only names arsenic and antimony. OUTSIDE REVIEW (two other AI reviewers, 2026-10-12): both chose the same answer as this key; they use general biology, not his key, so this does not remove the flag.

questions.stem: All these activities expose one to worm infections. Which of these guarantees worm infections?

options.text: Consuming (unfrozen and uncooked) wild animal meat raw.
Consuming salted, smoked, or frozen uncooked food.
Worming pet animals after adopting.
Walking barefoot on sand and soil.
Wading in lakes and shallow seas.

questions.answerRationale: Raw, unfrozen wild animal meat with no preservation processing at all carries the highest, least-mitigated risk - salting, smoking, and freezing are all recognized measures that actually kill many parasitic larvae, reducing (not guaranteeing) risk.

questions.stem: Which of these anthelmintic drugs directly or indirectly paralyzes worms?

options.text: Ivermectin and pyrantel pamoate.
Albendazole and praziquantel.
Piperazine citrate and mebendazole.
Niclosamide and bithionol.
All these drugs.

questions.answerRationale: The chapter's worm-drug table (§8.5.1) lists paralysis as the effect of every drug in it: ivermectin, piperazine, niclosamide, praziquantel and pyrantel 'cause paralysis', albendazole/benzimidazoles 'paralysis or death'. The stem says 'directly or indirectly', so All these drugs. The earlier key split the drugs by textbook mechanism and ignored the chapter's own table. OLQ 8 marked ivermectin + pyrantel wrong.

questions.stem: A veterinarian should not use _________ to treat flatworm infections and ________ in treating roundworm infections.

options.text: pyrantel pamoate/ niclosamide
piperazine citrate/ praziquantel
ivermectin/ albendazole

questions.answerRationale: Per the course chapter's worm-drug table (§8.5.1): pyrantel pamoate works on roundworms only and niclosamide on flatworms only, so each is the wrong drug for the other group. Option B is wrong because the chapter lists praziquantel as effective on flatworms AND roundworms - the earlier key treated it as flatworm-only (general pharmacology) instead of using the course's table. OLQ 8 marked B wrong.

questions.stem: A child is heavily infected with roundworms. Which of these is NOT a concern about this child while being treated for the infection in a clinic?

options.text: Allergic reactions to antigens released by the affected worms.
Movement of the worms may cause perforation of the intestine.
Accumulation of paralyzed worms may obstruct the intestine.
Uncontrolled muscle twitches in the child.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§8.5.1): pyrantel can cause intestinal obstruction from many paralyzed worms (C), and praziquantel's side effects come from immune reactions to antigens of dying worms (A). The text never describes muscle twitches in the host (D). Medium confidence: it also never mentions perforation (B), though that is a real clinical concern, so D rests on the text describing the drugs' muscle effects as acting on the worm. Confirmed correct on your second graded OLQ 8 attempt (19.5/20).

questions.stem: Which of these is drug synergy?

options.text: Additive efficacy and additive side effects.
Greater than additive efficacy but less than additive drug side effects.
Greater than additive efficacy and possibly greater than additive drug side effects.

questions.answerRationale: The strict pharmacological definition of synergy is about the therapeutic EFFICACY exceeding what simple addition would predict - it says nothing guaranteed about side effects, which could go either way, unlike the more optimistic (and less accurate) claim that synergy always means reduced combined toxicity.

questions.stem: Challenge Question: Which of the following antibiotic combinations is expected to be antagonistic?

options.text: Sulfa drugs and trimethoprim.
Methicillin (a beta-lactam antibiotic) and amikacin (an aminoglycoside).
Amoxycillin (a beta-lactam antibiotic) and chloramphenicol (protein synthesis inhibitor).

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§8.5.1): the antibacterial activities of beta-lactam drugs and chloramphenicol are considered antagonistic (beta-lactams need dividing cells; chloramphenicol stops growth).

questions.stem: Which of these is not a reason for combination therapy?

options.text: To aim at multiple targets of difficult-to-treat pathogens.
The drugs take advantage of the synergistic effect.
To use one drug to activate another (pro)drug.
To prevent bacterial drug resistance.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§8.5.1): reasons given are same-target synergy (sulfa + trimethoprim), multiple targets, and preventing resistance. Using one drug to activate another is not among them.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a drug toxicity, not a drug interaction?

options.text: Drug S binds to a plasma protein, increasing the blood level of the enzyme in the patient.
Drug R does not work if the patient drinks orange juice or a liquid antacid.
Drug Q increases the toxicity of drug Y if taken simultaneously.
Drug P reduces the efficacy of drug Y if taken simultaneously.
Drug T makes a person allergic to lip gloss and sunblock.

questions.answerRationale: The course (§8.5.2) defines a drug interaction as a drug's effect altered by ANOTHER chemical substance - 'other drugs, cosmetics, or food'. Option E (lip gloss and sunblock) is cosmetics, so it is an interaction; so are B (orange juice/antacid), C and D (a second drug). Only A has the drug acting on the patient with no second substance, which makes it the toxicity. The earlier key read E as a side effect and never noticed that cosmetics are in the course's list. OLQ 8 marked E wrong. A is the survivor by elimination. Confirmed correct on your second graded OLQ 8 attempt (19.5/20).

questions.stem: The MIC of an antibiotic is 20 micrograms/kg, which of the following is most likely the MBC for the same drug?

options.text: 20 micrograms/kg.
Less than 20 micrograms/kg.
More than 20 micrograms/kg.
It cannot be predicted from the information given.

questions.answerRationale: Fig. 8.23 of the chapter works an example with MIC 2 and MBC 4 micrograms/ml, so MBC is above MIC. Heads-up: §8.5.3 contains the sentence 'MIC is always higher than MBC', which contradicts its own figure and the definitions (MBC is the concentration that KILLS 99.9%). If your exam follows that sentence it would be B; the science and the figure say C. WHY NOT 100%: the science and Fig. 8.23 (MIC 2, MBC 4) say MBC is higher, so C. But §8.5.3 literally says 'MIC is always higher than MBC', and a professor who writes tricky questions from his own text could be keying B. OUTSIDE REVIEW (two other AI reviewers, 2026-10-12): both chose the same answer as this key; they use general biology, not his key, so this does not remove the flag.

questions.stem: Which of the following is INCORRECT about the Kirby-Bauer test for antibiotic susceptibility?

options.text: The test can be used to determine MBC but not MIC.
The test can only be done if an antibiotic is water-soluble.
The test can only be done if an antibiotic is stable in agar media.
It can test many antibiotics at once, but only on one bacterial strain at a time.
The zone of inhibition in the test indicates if a bacterium is sensitive or resistant to an antibiotic.

questions.answerRationale: The Kirby-Bauer disk diffusion test determines susceptibility category (and can estimate MIC via correlation charts) - it does not measure MBC at all, which requires separate quantitative broth/subculture methods, making this statement backwards.

questions.stem: A strain of bacteria can become resistant to an antibiotic to which it was once sensitive through each of the following processes. Which of the processes involves covalent drug modification?

options.text: The strain overexpresses efflux pump proteins.
The stain has a mutation in its rRNA gene or RNA polymerase gene.
The strain suppresses the synthesis of proteins that imports drug inside the cell.
The strain expresses a modified version (the second copy) of the target protein gene.
The strain expresses an enzyme that attaches an acetyl (CH3CO) group to an antibiotic.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (§8.5.4): CAT adds an acetyl group to chloramphenicol - 'a covalent modification of the drug'. Efflux, target mutation, reduced import and an alternative enzyme do not change the drug itself.

questions.stem: Challenge question: Which of the following mutations would make a bacterial strain resistant to aminoglycosides?

options.text: A mutation in the 16S rRNA gene.
A mutation in the 23S rRNA gene.
A mutation in the RNA polymerase gene.
A mutation in the DNA gyrase enzyme gene.
A mutation in the dihydrofolate synthase gene.

questions.answerRationale: Aminoglycosides bind 16S rRNA within the 30S ribosomal subunit, so a mutation there directly alters the drug's binding site and confers resistance.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most rapid method of spreading bacterial antibiotic resistance among different strains and species of pathogenic and nonpathogenic bacteria?

options.text: Gene mutations and vertical gene transfer.
Lateral gene transfer via bacterial conjugation.
Lateral gene transfer via bacterial transduction.
Lateral gene transfer via bacterial transformation.

questions.answerRationale: Conjugative plasmids, especially broad-host-range ones, transfer resistance genes efficiently across diverse bacterial species and strains, making conjugation the most rapid and significant driver of antibiotic resistance spread in clinical settings - more so than transduction (limited by phage host range) or transformation (limited to naturally competent species).

questions.stem: Which of the following is most likely the primary reason for bacterial antibiotic resistance in the developed countries of East Asia, Western Europe, Australia, and North America?

options.text: Use of antibiotics in treating non-bacterial infections.
Patient’s ability to purchase antibiotics without prescriptions.
Use of antibiotics in animal feed and fermentation industries.
Use of improper doses of antibiotics and use of expired/outdated antibiotics.

questions.answerRationale: Widespread subtherapeutic antibiotic use in industrial livestock and fermentation industries is a major, well-documented driver of resistance in developed nations, which typically otherwise enforce prescription requirements strictly (unlike less-regulated markets where over-the-counter purchase is the bigger issue).

questions.stem: According to the WHO, bacterial antibiotic resistance is currently at a crisis point, or human civilization is already in the post-antibiotic era. Which of the following is the most critical step nations would take to overcome this crisis?

options.text: Minimize antibiotic use.
Inactivate antibiotics before disposal.
Develop new and more effective antibiotics.
Stop agricultural and industrial use of antibiotics.
Rigorously enforce the drug laws and increase public education on antibiotic use.

questions.answerRationale: Course text (Table 8.14, 'Developing new antibiotics'): 'All the above measures may not eliminate bacterial strains that are already antibiotic-resistant ... some resistant strains retain the resistance even after growing in antibiotic-free conditions. Thus, at least some new and highly effective antibiotics are needed to eliminate those strains. ONCE THOSE STRAINS ARE UNDER CONTROL, rational use of antibiotics and public education may prevent another antibiotic crisis.' The stem says the crisis has ALREADY arrived ('currently at a crisis point, or ... already in the post-antibiotic era') and asks what is most critical to OVERCOME it, so new antibiotics (C); enforcement and public education only help prevent a repeat. The earlier key (E) was marked wrong on BOTH of your graded OLQ 8 attempts. WHY NOT 100%: Canvas only proves E is wrong. D (stop agricultural and industrial use) is the runner-up because OLQ 8 keys animal feed as the primary cause of resistance, and A (minimize use) is the first measure in Table 8.14. OUTSIDE REVIEW (two other AI reviewers, 2026-10-12): both chose the same answer as this key; they use general biology, not his key, so this does not remove the flag.
